en: Śrī! Salutations to the lotus feet of the venerable master Abhinava Nṛsiṃha Bhāratī, who is one with Śiva, the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.
The Crest-Jewel of Discrimination, with its Commentary.
(Dhyāna on Dakṣiṇāmūrti):
He who, desiring to lift up people submerged in the ocean of worldly existence,
manifested himself in the guise of the Guru Śivanṛsiṃha.
I constantly meditate in my heart upon that southern face, an ocean of compassion that dispels the darkness of ignorance.
(Prayer to Śāradā) O Goddess of Speech, whose nature is knowledge, worshipped at the feet of the Blessed One:
please expound from your own mouth the *Cūḍāmaṇi*, beginning with the *Viveka*.
O Śāradā, by your grace, may the profound meaning of the serene words of the Teacher and Lord shine within my heart.
(Prayer to Gaṇeśa) O Lord Gaṇeśa, whose womb contains jewels, the sun that dispels the darkness of obstacles;
O treasure-house of compassion, fulfill this exposition without impediment!
(Prayer to Candramaulīśvara) O Lord Candramaulīśvara, all-pervading one, who has taken refuge in the knowledge of Brahman,
you whose hand is adorned with the seal of consciousness— grant me your own direct experience immediately!

(Compendium of the Meaning of the Treatise) I bow down to that true Guru, Govinda, the supreme bliss, who is the object of the conclusions of all the Vedāntas, yet whose own nature is beyond the range of the senses. 1.
I bow down to that Govinda, the true Guru, who is the object of the conclusions of all Vedānta, yet who is himself beyond the reach of the senses, and who is supreme bliss.
(1) For living beings, human birth is difficult to attain; more so than that is manhood; and even more so than that is the status of a Brahmin.
Therefore, devotion to the path of Vedic dharma, scholarship,
the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, self-realization through direct experience, and abiding as one with Brahman—
liberation is not attained without the merits earned through hundreds of millions of births. ||2||

The human birth of living beings is rare; from that, manhood; from that, the status of a Brahmin; from that, devotion to the path of Vedic dharma; more difficult than this is true scholarship, the discrimination between the self and the non-self, personal realization, and abiding as one with the Brahman-Atman—liberation is not obtained without the merits earned through hundreds of millions of previous births. ||2||
A Sanskrit commentary graciously bestowed by Śrī Candraśekhara Bhāratī Svāmī, the Jagadguru of Śṛṅgeri:
In the Bhagavad Gītā— "You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom."
The wise do not grieve for those whose life has departed nor for those whose life has not yet departed.

This verse beginning with "jantūnām" (of living beings) serves as a summary of the entire subject matter expounded in the chapters of the *Vivekacūḍāmaṇi*, much like the opening verse [of the *Bhagavad Gītā*]. Since only an *āstika* (one who believes in the scriptures) has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this treatise, the author first suggests the existence of a self distinct from the body by means of praising the rarity of human birth: "For living beings, birth as a human is difficult to obtain.

As it is stated in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*: "In the scriptural practice, however, even though one acts with deliberation, one is not qualified [for the rites] without knowing the self's connection to the next world."

"For living beings" (*jantūnām*) means for creatures (*prāṇinām*) who are subject to birth; "human birth" (*narajanma*) means the state of being human (*mānuṣyakam*), which is difficult to obtain. In this regard, it is indeed possible to say that human birth is difficult to obtain among the many births one must undergo, because the word "birth" (*janma*) signifies the very connection with a body. And when there is a connection with multiple bodies for a single [being], the distinctness of the self (*ātman*) from the body is thereby indicated.

It is indeed well known that a thread joined with many flowers excels them; likewise, a body wearing many garments, whether successively or simultaneously, is distinct from them. Thus, for the attainment of a body that is a cause of happiness and for the cessation of a body that is a cause of suffering, engagement in merit and abstention from sin are appropriate. Therefore, only one who possesses faith (āstika) has the qualification for the scripture of action consisting of injunctions and prohibitions.
Similarly, this applies to the scripture of liberation as well, for the purpose of eliminating all karma through knowledge.

If the body alone were the self, then since that [body] is established through direct perception, how could the injunctions for the means of seeing—such as, "The self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"—be justified? Furthermore: "Through auspicious deeds one attains divinity; through prohibited ones, a hellish body;
through both merit and demerit, one helplessly obtains human birth."

Thus, it is shown that by means of virtuous, non-virtuous, and mixed actions, a single individual alone acquires bodies of different types. Otherwise, how could the variety of happiness, suffering, and so forth, well-known in the world, be accounted for? If the Lord were to create some living beings happy and others otherwise, independent of karma, he would incur partiality and cruelty; and in that case, his status as the Lord would be lost.

This has been stated in the sūtras: "There is no inequality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He is dependent [on karma]; for thus Scripture shows"; "If it be argued that [the world] could not exist because of the non-differentiation of karma, we say no, because of its beginninglessness"; and "It is both logical and observed. By these sūtras, the dependence of the Lord on karma and the beginninglessness of saṃsāra are established. If saṃsāra itself, as a state of being, is beginningless, then the beginninglessness of the transmigrating soul who is its substratum is established by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so).

Thus, it is established that the self is distinct from the body; one who asserts the existence of a self distinct from the body is an *āstika*. It has been indicated by the statement "human birth is difficult for living beings to obtain" that *āstikya* (the state of being an āstika) is the very foundation of engagement with the scriptures.

From that [study], manhood [is attained]; for since women lack the qualification for the Veda, the Self—which is to be realized solely through the Upaniṣads—cannot be known by them; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, although members of the three higher castes possess the qualification for the Veda, because Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are engaged in external activities such as governing a kingdom or agriculture—which cause distraction of the mind—it is difficult for them to engage in the inquiry into the Self with primary intent. Thus: "This duty of bearing the Vaiṣṇava mark is prescribed for those born from the mouth [of Brahmā]; it is not ordained for those born from the arms or the thighs."

Thus, according to the Smṛti, because there is scope for renunciation—which is the primary means for the inquiry into Brahman—attainment of Brahman within a single birth is difficult for those two [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya] to achieve. To highlight this, instead of saying "then twice-bornness" (*dvijatvam tataḥ*), it says "then Brahminhood" (*tato vipratā*).
Indeed, for a Brāhmaṇa, this body is not intended for enjoyment;
it leads to great suffering in this world and to infinite happiness after death.

Thus, according to the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti, the sense is that it is possible for a Brāhmaṇa to attain Brahman in this very life by performing the duties of engagement and renunciation ordained by the Vedas.

For this very reason, it is said that one must be devoted to the path of Vedic dharma. The sense is that what is to be attained is not obtained merely by being a Brahmin, but rather by attaining that status and then performing the duties appropriate to it. According to the Śruti, "Dharma is the foundation of the entire world... through dharma one dispels evil," it is dharma alone that is the means to happiness, the remover of evil which is the cause of suffering, and, by removing that [evil], the cause of the absence of suffering. Thus, [the desire arises]: "May happiness be mine; may suffering not be mine."

In order to indicate that he alone is the means for achieving the human goals (puruṣārtha) consisting of happiness—the object of the desires of all people—and the absence of suffering, [the author] uses the term "dharma. By the etymologies "that which sustains" (dhārayati) or "that by which one is sustained" (dhriyate 'nena), it is intended to suggest that his status as the cause of the world's foundation is taught by the Śruti; thus, rather than saying "on the path of Vedic rituals," it is said "on the path of dharma."

Even though Vedic ritual action (*vaidika-karman*) is indeed *dharma*, the intended meaning is not captured by the mere word "action" (*karman*). If there were some means for achieving happiness or removing suffering that existed apart from *dharma*, then everyone in the world would certainly be happy and free from suffering at all times simply by procuring those means.

However, since *dharma* is supersensible (*atīndriya*) and can be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*), it is possible to demonstrate that because people lack knowledge of it without the scriptures, they fail to obtain the means and consequently fail to obtain the fruit. Thus it is said: "Vedic... and so forth.

Regarding the definition of Dharma, the great sage Jaimini formulated the aphorism: "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*). That it is based on the authority of the Vedas is understood through the qualifying term "Vedic" (*vaidika*). Indeed, apart from the Veda, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is capable of establishing itself regarding the subject of Dharma; for since Dharma is supersensuous (*atīndriya*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) has no scope there. For this very reason, inference (*anumāna*) does not apply to it, because the operation of inference is rooted in perception.

For this very reason, even words other than the Veda are incapable of making that [Dharma] known. Since the Smṛtis are of human origin, there is the possibility of error, negligence, and so forth on the part of their authors; thus, because of the suspicion of invalidity based on defects in the author, their authority must be asserted as being rooted solely in the Śruti, which—being non-human—is untainted by even a scent of defect. Consequently, any word other than the Veda lacks intrinsic validity regarding Dharma.

Furthermore, how did the authors of the Smṛtis know the supersensuous Dharma? If you say it was through the power born of Yoga, then how was that power acquired by them? If you say it was through the performance of Dharma, then how was that Dharma known? Precisely for this reason [it is said]:
"He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him..."

Thus, the Śruti teaches that even for Hiraṇyagarbha, who was being created at the beginning, knowledge of Dharma is rooted solely in the Veda as favored by the Lord. What then need be said regarding others? Therefore, it is well said that [Dharma] is "Vedic. By the expression "subsisting on water" or "subsisting on air," the Śruti indicates that Dharma is knowable through the Veda alone. Here, by the word "Dharma," both the dharma of engagement (pravṛtti-dharma) and the dharma of withdrawal (nivṛtti-dharma) are meant. For it is stated in the Gītā-bhāṣya: "Indeed, the Dharma declared in the Veda is of two kinds: characterized by engagement and characterized by withdrawal."

The followers of Karma-mīmāṃsā maintain that Dharma alone is the supreme means for attaining eternal happiness and that nothing else need be sought. The author casts a glance at them with the word "path" (mārga). By this, he indicates that while the duty of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), in the form of renunciation itself, is required as the cause for the inquiry into the Vedānta—which is the means for the direct realization of Brahman that serves as the instrument for the supreme human goal—and while the duty of engagement (*pravṛtti-dharma*), in the form of the performance of desireless action, is required as the cause for the purity of mind which is the cause of dispassion toward those [worldly] means; yet it is not [the case that... [text continues].
It is thus indicated that both of these are the direct means for attaining unsurpassed bliss. As it was stated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa:
"Now, there are these two paths upon which the Vedas are established:
dharma characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and that proclaimed as renunciation (nivṛtti)."

And thus: "After initiation, let the Brāhmaṇa constantly study the Veda; let him perform the rituals prescribed therein; let him offer worship to the Lord through them; and let his mind abandon desire for optional rites."
Let the flood of evil be shaken off, and let your attention be fixed upon the happiness of existence.
Let your own desire be resolved; depart quickly from your own home.
Association with the virtuous should be cultivated; firm devotion to the Blessed One should be established;
peace and other virtues should be thoroughly mastered; and worldly action should be swiftly and most firmly renounced.

Thus, it has been taught that by performing actions with the understanding of offering them to the Lord according to the method prescribed in the *Sopānapañcaka*, one should purify the mind, become detached from sense objects, and desist from ritual actions. As it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*: "There is no wealth for a Brāhmaṇa such as oneness, equanimity, truthfulness, good conduct, steadfastness, laying aside the rod of punishment, straightforwardness, and then, above all, withdrawal from ritual activities."
The state of being a knower (*vidvattva*) is superior to that.

In this regard, concerning the sphere of *pravṛtti-dharma* (active duty), the application is as follows: by the *Chāndogya* Śruti passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful," it is taught that if an action being performed is preceded by the knowledge of the meaning of the mantras that constitute its constituent parts, it leads to a greater fruit.

This has been stated in the commentary on that very point: "For it is seen in the world that in the sale of rubies by a merchant and a Śabara, the merchant’s superiority in result arises from his superior knowledge. Regarding the subject of the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*), since there is the injunction, "Having renounced, one should engage in hearing (*śravaṇa*"), "the state of being a knower" (*vidvatva*) consists in possessing indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) produced by hearing the Vedānta texts subsequent to renunciation. This [knowledge] is the discrimination between the Supreme Self and the non-Self. This will be clarified later in the text itself.

By this, *manana* (reflection) is described as consisting of contemplation through logical reasoning for the purpose of strengthening the meaning of what has been heard (*śruta*), thereby dispelling doubts and misconceptions.

From that follows *svānubhava* (self-experience), which is stated to be the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman preceded by *nididhyāsana* (meditative absorption). For this very reason, it is called "self-experience," because the experience arising from *śravaṇa* and *manana* does not attain excellence in the absence of *nididhyāsana*, which removes contrary impressions (*viparītabhāvanā*). By this, the four stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*) have been described: *śubhecchā* (pure desire), *vicāraṇā* (investigation), *tanumānasā* (thinned mind), and *sattvāpatti* (attainment of being).

Non-attachment (*asaṃsakti*), the non-contemplation of objects (*padārthābhāvanā*), and the state beyond the fourth (*turyagā*)—which is "establishment as Brahman and the Self" (*brahmātmanā saṃsthitiḥ*)—are indicated here by the word *saṃsthiti*. This term signifies one’s own direct experience (*svānubhava*) accompanied by the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). By this, it is also suggested that *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya* do not constitute primary liberation (*mukhyamukti*), because all four of these pertain to the qualified (*saguṇa*) [Brahman] and are therefore illusory (*mithyā*); for the nature of Brahman, which consists in being devoid of the three limitations (*paricchedatrayaśūnyatva*), is impossible in the qualified [Brahman].

The connection is as follows: liberation (mukti) is indeed isolation (kaivalya), which is the state of abiding in one's own nature as the absolute Brahman—devoid of the relationship with all imagined kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and characterized by being eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), and perfectly full; this is not obtained without the merits performed over hundreds of millions of births. ||2||
These three things are indeed difficult to obtain, being caused by the grace of the gods:
human birth, the desire for liberation, and reliance upon a Great Being. (3)
The sequence is as follows: human birth, the desire for liberation, and reliance upon a Great Being—this triad, caused by divine grace, is indeed difficult to obtain. ||3||
Having somehow attained the rare birth as a human, and therein even manhood and the ability to perceive the further shore of the Vedas,
that person of deluded intellect who does not strive for the liberation of his own self— [he is truly lost].
He is a destroyer of himself, for through his false grasping he slays his own self.

Having somehow obtained this human birth, which is difficult to attain, and even therein manhood and the ability to see the further shore of the Vedas, that fool who does not strive for the liberation of his own self is a destroyer of himself; through his attachment to the unreal, he slays his own soul. 4.

Who is there more deluded than this person who, having obtained a human body so difficult to attain—and even therein the capacity for human effort—yet remains negligent regarding his own true welfare? (5)
Who else here is so deluded as he who, having obtained this rare human body and even therein the power of human effort, yet neglects his own true interest? (5)
Let them study the scriptures, let them sacrifice to the gods, let them perform rituals, and let them worship the deities;
yet without the realization of the identity of the Self, there is no liberation.
It is not accomplished even within a hundred Brahmās. ||6||

Let them study the scriptures, let them worship the gods, let them perform rituals, and let them honor the deities; yet without the realization of the oneness of the Self, liberation is not achieved even within hundreds of millions of Brahmās. (6)
For the Śruti clearly declares: "There is no hope for immortality through wealth," since it thus makes explicit that ritual action is not the cause of liberation.
The sequence is as follows: since it is clear that action is not the cause of liberation, for the Śruti indeed declares, "One does not hope for immortality through wealth. (7)

The Commentary: Since human birth, personal effort, and so forth are attainable only through the excellence of merit accumulated over many births; since a person must remain vigilant regarding their own true welfare; and since liberation—which consists of the absolute cessation of suffering and unsurpassed bliss—does not manifest directly through the collection of ritual acts such as the study and performance of the *Karmakāṇḍa* without the realization of the identity of the Self; and since the Śruti itself explicitly states this matter regarding actions accomplished by wealth: "There is no hope for immortality through wealth."
"Direct utility for liberation has been established through perception; therefore, the wise person should strive for liberation"—
thus, the wise person, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects, should strive for liberation.
Having approached a peaceful and great teacher, his self is composed through the meaning taught by him. ||8||

Therefore, the wise person, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects, should strive for liberation; having approached a virtuous and great teacher, he should direct his self toward the goal taught by that teacher. (8)
Commentary:
By "the wise one," one who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal is meant.
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the sources of suffering.
They have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them.

Thus, because this meaning has been indicated by the word *budha* (the wise) in the Gītā, the phrase *bāhyārtha* (external objects) illuminates the impermanence of sensual pleasure. Since external objects are adventitious and lack constancy, the manifestation of the pleasure derived from them is likewise characterized by that same nature. Therefore, a discerning person of foremost character must abandon desire for such things; first, he states the method of effort required: "having abandoned the longing for the pleasure of external objects."

"External" refers to those objects which are external; "external objects" (bāhyārtha) means those things. "Happiness from external objects" (bāhyārthasukha) is happiness derived from them. Longing for that is "longing for happiness from external objects" (bāhyārthasukhaspṛhā). He by whom this has been renounced is described as one who is dispassionate toward the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to both this world and the next. By this, it is essentially stated that his inner self (svānta) has been rendered utterly pure through the performance of actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti without desire for rewards.

The word "san" (being) indicates that for one who lacks discrimination and is greedy for sense-objects, even mere existence is difficult to attain. According to the Śruti—"A man who has a teacher knows"—and "From the teacher alone is knowledge obtained; it reaches its highest perfection," since the identity with the Self, which transcends the senses, cannot be realized without a Guru, one must take refuge in a Great Person in the manner previously described. This is stated by the words beginning with "san. The meaning is: "He who exists" (*asti*)—that is, *san*—him [one should seek].

"If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. "That which is the Plenum (bhūman), that is the Immortal; everything else is perishable. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.
"The existence of the non-existent is not found, nor is the non-existence of the existent found.
The limit of both has been perceived by those who see the truth."

Because of such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*), existence (*astitva*)—defined as being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—belongs to Brahman alone. The teacher’s possession of that same nature follows from his non-difference from Him, according to the scripture: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself. By this, the steadfastness in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*), characterized by the complete cessation of identification with unreal, non-self entities, is indicated.

"Desiring to know That, one should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman"; and from such scriptural passages as, "There is no way to this [knowledge] unless it is taught by another; for it is subtler than the subtlest, beyond the reach of logic. For it is only from such a Guru that the pure realization of the Self—free from doubt, mental construction, and the like—is possible.

Indeed, this is logical: even in the world, a path not seen by us must be pointed out by those who have seen that path; and even if something is somehow discovered by oneself, any doubt regarding it must be dispelled by those who have perceived its true nature.

In this regard, the dialogue between Śuka and Janaka serves as authoritative evidence. For it is recorded in the *Vāsiṣṭha* and other texts that although Śuka had himself realized the object of knowledge through the ripening of merits performed in previous births, he nevertheless came to rest his mind in Brahman at the word of his father, the high-souled Janaka, the King of Videha, even though he had already been instructed by him. Thus, because he is non-different from Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*), the Guru also possesses the nature of Being. For this very reason, he possesses greatness. Because the five sheaths (*kośapañcaka*) have been analyzed and discarded, he is unlimited (*aparicchinna*).
Alternatively, he is adorned with all the excellent qualities mentioned in the scriptures. As will be stated:
He is a master of the Vedas, free from vice, and unassailed by desire; he is the supreme knower of Brahman, an ocean of causeless compassion, and a kinsman to the virtuous who bow before him.

"One who is tranquil in Brahman, peaceful, like a fire without fuel"—such is the collection of qualities [described]. He is a *deśika* (guide) because he imparts knowledge to disciples; having approached him according to the prescribed rule (*yathāvidhi*) and having attended upon him, one whose self—that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is properly fixed on that very object taught by that Guru, which consists of the nature of Brahman as well as the means for attaining it, should strive for liberation. By the phrase "should strive for liberation," the state of being a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣutva*) is implied, since effort toward that end is impossible without a desire for liberation.

By the phrase "one whose self is concentrated on the taught meaning," it is stated that since a mind constantly absorbed in Brahman is impossible without the renunciation of all actions, a person of discrimination who is dispassionate must approach a Guru established in Brahman—having first renounced all actions by their very nature—and always engage in inquiry into Brahman. ||8||

He explains the meaning briefly stated [in the previous verse] with seven verses. Therein, since the effort exerted for the sake of liberation culminates in the perfection of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), he states in this verse the perfection of right vision as the direct means to liberation and, as its primary cause, the state of being established in yoga (*yogārūḍhatva*), which is synonymous with supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya*): "Having attained the state of being established in yoga through steadfastness in right vision, one should uplift oneself by means of the self when it has sunk into the ocean of saṃsāra. (9)

The sequence is as follows: having attained the state of being established in yoga, one should, through steadfastness in right vision, uplift by means of the self the self that has been submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. ||9||
The Commentary:
For when one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions,
having renounced all volitions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.
Thus, from the words of the Blessed One,
the meaning is that steadfastness in right vision preceded by supreme detachment alone is the cause for uplifting the self fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra.
[The mind] is joined with the waves of the fivefold afflictions and the like, and is full of delusion.

Having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra— which is infested with the crocodiles of wife, son, acquired wealth, and kinsmen, and which is filled with the net of the bodiless god of love whose fire is like the submarine conflagration— I go unto Hari.

O Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, grant me the support of Your hand to me, who am struggling in the struggle against being swallowed by the fierce crocodiles and sea-monsters of Time in the vast ocean of saṃsāra, and who am tormented by the fish of the multitude of passions.

In this manner, because saṃsāra—which consists of ignorance and its manifestations—is difficult to cross without perfect knowledge, it is metaphorically described as an ocean. For one who regards the non-self body as the Self, it is impossible to realize that when the body is born or dies, its attributes do not belong to oneself; nor can one realize this regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) when it is afflicted by hunger and thirst, or regarding the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) when it experiences pleasure or pain.

Thus, because ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*) are continuous, the five afflictions and so forth are metaphorically described as waves. It is clear that delusion itself is delusion; the very notion of something in what is not that is the whirlpool, and so on. Due to beginningless ignorance, the ignorant person—thinking "I am an agent," "I am a man," and so forth—remains identified with the gross, subtle, and causal bodies which are non-self. This state of failing to attain one's true nature is indeed immersion in the ocean of *saṃsāra* for the Self, whose nature is unattached, consciousness, and bliss. Even in that regard, [it persists] during deep sleep.

Since cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is not experienced [by the Self], it must be stated that its very root lies in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the form of the mind of one who lacks discrimination. For it is heard in scripture:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense-objects, it leads to bondage; free from objects, it is declared to lead to liberation."
Therefore, it is the mind, devoid of discrimination, that is attached to the body and so forth; it is the self that is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.

Therefore, when the mind becomes refined by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by scriptural study such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), it then becomes free from error through the attainment of knowledge of the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya-jñāna*). One should uplift the undiscriminating mind—that is, one should withdraw it from non-Self objects—by means of a mind endowed with discrimination born of the scriptures. Furthermore, because of its inherent tendency toward extroversion, the mind is attached to external things such as the body; thus, although the Self is in reality unattached, it appears as if attached, like a crystal appearing red [due to proximity with a red object]. Of such a Self, [one should uplift the mind].

The sense is that when there is an absence of connection with the non-self due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and when one is established solely in the Self by being turned inward, the Self becomes as if uplifted.

The syntactical connection is: having attained the state of being established in yoga, one should uplift the Self—which is submerged in the ocean of worldly existence—by means of the Self through steadfastness in right vision. ||9||

Clarifying the state of being established in yoga, he first describes hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption—which follow renunciation—as the means for attaining steadfastness in perfect realization, beginning with the words "having renounced":
"Having renounced all actions for the sake of liberation from the bondage of worldly existence, let the wise and steadfast ones, intent upon the practice of the Self, strive. (10)
Having renounced all actions, let the wise and steadfast who have approached [this path] strive in the practice of the Self for liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. (10)
The Commentary:

Having renounced all actions—those prescribed in the *Karmakāṇḍa*—and having abandoned them even in their essential nature, for the sake of liberation from the bondage of worldly existence (*bhava-bandha*), that is, for the sake of steadfastness in right vision (*samyag-darśana*) which is the cause for the cessation of the bonds of transmigratory life; by the "wise" (*paṇḍitaḥ*), meaning those possessing indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) regarding the Self, and by the "steadfast" (*dhīraiḥ*), meaning those who have brought their intellects under control—the Self-existent One (*svayambhūḥ*) pierced the openings directed outward.
Therefore, one looks outward and not at the inner self;
but some wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inward self with his gaze turned back.

Thus says the Śruti. One who bestows wisdom (*dhī*) is called *dhīra*; when it is said that he brings the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the primary element among the aggregate of causes and effects, under his control, the conquest of the other senses is established as a matter of course. By this, his possession of tranquility and other such qualities is indicated.
For this very reason, regarding the practice of the Self: "Meditating upon That, speaking of That, and mutually awakening one another to That."
And the wise know that single-minded devotion to this is the practice of Brahman.

According to the saying of the learned, "one should strive by means of the practice of *nididhyāsana*—which consists of a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions unimpeded by heterogeneous ones—by those who are present and engaged in the activities described in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, namely reflecting upon what has been heard, explaining it, and mutually awakening one another. For such a person, it should be understood that the state of being established in *yoga* (the synonym for supreme detachment) is already accomplished through the renunciation of all volitional thoughts (*saṃkalpa*). ||10||

If it be objected that, since scriptural injunctions such as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa rites as long as one lives," "One should worship the twilight devotions day by day," and "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years" enjoin the performance of action throughout one's life, it would follow that renouncing all actions constitutes a transgression of the scriptures—[we reply] that those scriptures have as their subject matter the person whose mind is not yet purified.

For this very reason, the *Īśāvāsya* mantra states: "Thus for you, and not otherwise, there is no other path; action does not cling to the man. This means that for "you"—that is, for one who identifies as a mere human—there is no other way than this performance of action that serves to prevent the clinging of karma. [As it is said: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality; the self-controlled ascetics of purified being, through the yoga of renunciation."
For these eighteen forms of sacrifice, in which ritual action is said to be inferior, are but rafts that are unstable. Fools are they who rejoice in this as the highest good.
They return once again to old age and death.

Because the renunciation of action is also enjoined by such statements as, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? and because action is censured [in other passages].

By reflecting on the meaning of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self," it is determined that these [rites] serve as means for the desire to know (vividiṣā) by way of purifying the mind, but not that they must be performed perpetually.

If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with scriptural injunctions prescribing renunciation, such as, "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," as well as the incongruity of the censure of ritual action (*karman*). For this very reason, this same point is stated in the two Sūtras: "And therefore, there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires, etc. and "There is dependence on all [actions], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Ritual actions do not have liberation—which is the supreme human goal—as their direct purpose; rather, they serve as an external aid to knowledge by way of purifying the mind. This is what he expresses with the words beginning with "of the mind": [The text continues: "Of the mind... and so forth.

Having renounced all actions prescribed in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and having abandoned them even in their essential nature, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence—that is, for the sake of steadfastness in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the cause for the cessation of the fetters of *saṃsāra*—by the wise (*paṇḍitaḥ*), who possess indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding the Self, and by the steadfast (*dhīraiḥ*), whose intellects are self-controlled; for it is said:
"The Self-existent One pierced the openings [of the senses] outward;
therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self."

"A certain wise man beheld the inner Self, with his eyes turned inward, desiring immortality"—so says the Śruti. He is "wise" (dhīra) because he bestows (rāti) wisdom; when it is said that he brings the intellect (buddhi)—which is the primary factor among the aggregate of cause and effect—under his control, the conquest of the other senses is established as a matter of course. By this, it is indicated that he is endowed with tranquility and other such qualities.
Therefore, regarding the practice of the Self:
"Thinking of That, speaking of That, mutual awakening to That,
and being solely intent upon That— this is what the wise know as the practice of Brahman."

According to the saying of the learned, "one should strive by means of the practice of *nididhyāsana*—which consists of a continuous flow of similar mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya*) unobstructed by heterogeneous impressions (*vijātīya-pratyaya*)—by those who are present and engaged in the activities described in the *jñāna-kāṇḍa*, namely reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard, explaining it, and mutually awakening one another. For such a person, it should be understood that the state of being established in yoga (*yogārūḍhatva*), which is synonymous with supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*), is already accomplished through the renunciation of all volitional thoughts (*sarvasaṅkalpa-saṃnyāsa*). ||10||

If it be objected that, because such scriptural injunctions as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives," "One should worship the twilight [Sandhyā] daily," and "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years" enjoin the performance of action for the duration of one's life, it would follow that renouncing all actions constitutes a transgression of the scriptures—[we reply: no, for those scriptures have as their object those whose minds are not yet purified.

For this very reason, the *Īśāvāsya* mantra states: "Thus for you, and not otherwise, there is no path; action does not cling to the man. This means that for you—the one who identifies as a mere man—there is no other way than this performance of action that can serve as the cause for the non-clinging of action.

[As the same text continues: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality; the self-controlled ones, whose being is purified through the yoga of renunciation."
For these eighteen forms of sacrifice, in which ritual action is said to be inferior, are but rafts that are unstable. Fools are they who rejoice in this as the highest good.
They return once again to old age and death.

Because the renunciation of action has been enjoined by such statements as, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? and because action has been censured [in other passages].

By reflecting on the meaning of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self," it is determined that these [rites] serve as means for the desire to know (vividiṣā) by way of purifying the mind, but not that they must be performed at all times.

If that were the case, it would result in a contradiction of the injunctions prescribing renunciation, such as, "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," as well as the inconsistency of the censure of ritual action (*karman*). For this very reason, this same point is stated in the two *sūtras*: "And therefore there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires, etc. and "There is dependence on all [actions], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Ritual actions do not have liberation—the supreme human goal—as their purpose; rather, they serve as an external aid to knowledge by means of purifying the mind. This is what he expresses with the words "of the mind":
"Ritual action is for the purification of the mind, but not for the apprehension of reality."
The establishment of reality occurs through investigation; it cannot be achieved by millions of ritual acts.
Practice is for the purification of the mind, not for the apprehension of an object; the establishment of an object occurs through investigation, and not by millions of practices. (11)
The meaning is clear.
He clarifies that investigation is the cause for perceiving the reality of an object by means of an illustration, beginning with "properly":
"Through proper investigation, the ascertainment of the true nature of the rope is established."
She destroys the suffering caused by the great serpent arisen from delusion. ||12||
The ascertainment of the reality of the rope, established through correct investigation, destroys the suffering and fear of the great serpent produced by delusion. || 12 ||
Commentary:

It is well known that a person who, in dim darkness, mistakes a rope lying there for a snake and becomes afraid, abandons the suffering of fear, trembling, and so forth, upon bringing a lamp and correctly investigating until he realizes the true nature of the object. In that case, the great snake which arose through delusion regarding the rope—the suffering produced by that [delusory] cognition—is destroyed by the ascertainment of the reality of the rope, which is produced by correct investigation.

Similarly, the suffering of existence—the suffering brought about by birth and death—which has arisen through delusion, is destroyed by the ascertainment of reality, which is produced by right inquiry; this is the realization of the true nature of the Self, the direct intuition of Brahman. Thus, this illustration is useful in every respect for the subject at hand. ||12||

He states that only an investigation conducted in accordance with the words of a reliable authority (āpta) is the cause for the ascertainment of an object, and no other action is so; thus he says: "Of the object...
The ascertainment of an object is seen to arise from an investigation based on beneficial instruction.
Neither by bathing, nor by giving gifts, nor even by a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
The determination of the truth is seen to arise from beneficial instruction and inquiry, not from ritual bathing, nor from giving gifts, nor even from hundreds of breath-restraints. || 13 ||
Commentary:

For a person who is himself deluded by the power of the defect of ignorance, since it is difficult for him to engage in inquiry on his own while experiencing misfortunes such as fear and trembling in the absence of a support in the form of the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*), the beneficial instruction is made the cause for inquiry. And "beneficiality" consists in speaking according to reality.

The sense is this: if a person in error, instead of engaging in inquiry according to the instruction for their welfare, performs such acts as bathing, giving gifts, or a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), how could they become one whose misfortune has ceased? For in the absence of immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*) that removes delusion, the delusion which causes misfortune does not cease. Furthermore, "inquiry" (*vicāra*) is a mental activity conducive to the ascertainment of the true nature of reality.

And likewise, it is established by perception in cases of error that it is only inquiry assisted by beneficial instruction that serves as the cause for valid knowledge of an object. This being so, in the present case as well, the instruction is that one should perform inquiry into the Self in accordance with the teachings of the Śruti and the preceptor, realize its true nature through direct intuition, and thereby liberate the Self from saṃsāra, which consists of the superimposition of the non-Self. ||13||

Since only one who is capable of a particular action can possibly be the enjoyer of the fruit of that action, whereas for one who lacks such capacity it is impossible, [the author] states that external factors such as place and time possess only the status of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), while internal capacity alone is the bestower of the fruit: "He [the Lord] blesses the qualified person... "The attainment of the fruit especially blesses the qualified person;
means such as place and time are its auxiliaries in this regard. (14)
The logical connection is as follows:
in this [system], place, time, and so forth, the accomplishment of the fruit, and especially the qualified practitioner, the means, and the auxiliary factors are all present. 14.
Commentary:

Since ritual actions (*karma*) have visible purposes, one must admit that place and time are also uncommon causes, in accordance with scriptural injunctions such as: "One offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," "One offers at the horse's footprint," "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east," "One offers in the evening," "One offers in the morning," "One should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma* every spring," and "One should establish the sacred fires in the spring.
This is true even for knowledge (*jñāna*).

As it is in a mirror, so it is in the self; as it is in a dream, so it is in the world of the ancestors. As if clearly seen in water, so it is in the world of the Gandharvas; as in shadow and light, so it is in the world of Brahmā.
"In this world, if one has known [the Self], then there is truth; if one has not known it here, there is great ruin.
According to such scriptural passages, it is understood that only the human world and the world of Brahmā constitute the stages for knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmi*). Thus...
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
for he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes to perdition.

According to such authoritative texts as, "Having completed the stage of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); and from there, one should renounce," it appears that even for *saṃnyāsa*, which is an internal means to the knowledge of Brahman, a specific time is prescribed. Nevertheless, the king of the Rākṣasas, Virocana, though his mind was impure, did not grasp the Self even after reaching the world of Brahmā and being instructed by the Supreme Preceptor, Parameṣṭhin. For it is said: "Those who have attained supreme detachment renounce the world without even performing marriage, having seen that worldly existence itself is devoid of essence and desiring to perceive the true essence."

By such scriptural authorities as, "Or else, one may renounce even from the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), or from the householder's life, or from the forest-dweller's life; on whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," the intention is that for one who is endowed with the fourfold means—beginning with the aforementioned detachment—the specific time and place are not intended [as restrictive]; thus, their status as auxiliary factors has been stated.

For this very reason, in the passage beginning with "the wise man, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects," the two factors of discernment (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) are established as the causes for the concentration of the mind upon the subject matter taught by a Guru—preceded by approaching such a Guru who instructs in the means to liberation—for the sake of attaining right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the direct cause of liberation characterized by abiding as Brahman-Ātman.

Since such concentration of the mind is impossible in the absence of tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), withdrawal (*uparati*), forbearance (*titikṣā*), and faith (*śraddhā*), and because effort for that purpose cannot occur in the absence of a desire for liberation, the first verse beginning with "Therefore, for the sake of liberation" has already indicated the common causes for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*): discrimination (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), the sixfold set beginning with tranquility (*śamādi-ṣaṭka*), and the state of seeking liberation (*mumukṣutva*).

And thus, in accordance with such scriptural passages as "He crosses over sorrow" and "For the sake of knowing That, one should approach a Guru alone," right knowledge—which destroys the bondage denoted by the word 'sorrow'—is not attained by any other means whatsoever without the inquiry into the subject matter taught by a true Guru. In this verse, the word *asyām* (in this) has the meaning of *siddhau* (in the accomplishment). ||14||
Therefore, having approached a compassionate ocean, a Guru who is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, the seeker of the reality of the Self must engage in inquiry. (15)
Therefore, having approached a Guru who is an ocean of compassion and the highest among the knowers of Brahman, one who desires to know must perform an inquiry into the reality of the Self. ||15||
Commentary:

Therefore, because it is the cause of the definitive knowledge that removes all misfortunes, the investigation of the reality of the Self must be undertaken by the seeker—a person desiring to know the Self correctly. Regarding this, he states the procedure to be followed: [one should approach] the Ocean of Compassion. By virtue of having achieved his own purpose, the Master’s lack of personal need for anything is already established; yet, out of compassion—meaning an ocean of pity—he thinks, "May others also not experience suffering. The word "ocean" (sindhu) signifies a reservoir, just as a mass of water is a reservoir of waters. [He approaches] the Guru: the syllable *gu* refers to darkness (*andhakāra*), and the syllable *ru* refers to that which obstructs it.
Because he has brought about the cessation of darkness, he is designated as "the Guru."

Thus, according to the manner stated by the Guru-gītā, the meaning is that [the teaching] removes the internal darkness known as ignorance (*ajñāna*) through its own instruction. Just as darkness, having enveloped the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), becomes an obstacle to the knowledge of it, so too ignorance, having enveloped the Self (*ātman*), becomes an obstacle to its clear manifestation; such is the "darkness-nature" of ignorance. For this very reason, it is designated by words such as "darkness" (*tamas*) in the Śruti, as in passages such as: "Darkness indeed existed, hidden by darkness in the beginning."

He describes that person in whom these two qualifications are possible as "the best among the knowers of Brahman" (*brahmaviduttama*). Those who know Brahman are the "knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*); the meaning is "the best among them," namely, the one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*). The scriptural passages regarding this have been cited previously.
And the means of attaining him is stated thus: "Having propitiated that Guru with devotion, being humble through service and humility," according to the method that will be explained hereafter.

"Know that through prostration, inquiry, and service"—according to this teaching of the *Gītā*, one's own Self is brought face-to-face. Thus, the explanation of the eighth verse, beginning with "for the sake of liberation," has been completed by means of these [subsequent] verses. ||15||
The wise man, learned and skilled in reasoning and refutation, who is characterized by the aforementioned marks, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self. ||16||

The logical connection is as follows: a person who is learned, wise, and skilled in the process of reasoning through inclusion and exclusion (ūha-apoha), and who is characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā). || 16 ||
The Commentary:
It was stated that "the attainment of the fruit especially awaits the qualified person"; now, with the words beginning with "medhāvī," he describes the qualified person in the present context.

According to the *Kośa* (Amara-kośa), which states "medhā is wisdom endowed with retention," one who possesses the intellect capable of retaining the meaning of what has been heard is called *medhāvī*; by the etymology "one who has *medhā*," the word *medhāvī* denotes a learned person. One who has studied poetry, lexicons, and grammar is so described. By the phrase "skilled in reasoning and refutation" (*ūhāpohavicakṣaṇaḥ*), it is understood that his intellect is refined by logic (*tarka*) and hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*).

"An expert in words, sentences, and means of valid knowledge" (padavākyapramāṇajña) means one who is characterized by the definitions stated [previously]. This refers to one who, as indicated by the verses occurring from the eighth up to the fifteenth śloka—both in summary and in detail—is endowed with the fourfold means consisting of discrimination, dispassion, the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama), and the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva). Such a person is qualified for the science of the Self (ātmavidyā); that is to say, he is fit to experience liberation, which is the fruit of the science of the Self. ||16||

The characteristics have been stated; now, having embraced them for the sake of clear understanding, he says "for the discerning one. Alternatively, the characteristic that has been stated is the state of desiring to know.

Regarding the statement, "One who desires to know the reality of the Self must practice *atovicāra*," it is precisely such a seeker—distinguished by qualities such as intelligence—who partakes in the fruit of the knowledge of the Self. If one asks, "Who is qualified for this inquiry at present? [the author] replies with the word "of the discerning one" (*vivekinaḥ*), referring to one who was previously described in the eighth verse as "the wise man who has renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects and whose mind is concentrated on the taught subject," and in the tenth verse as indicated by the word "by the steadfast ones" (*dhīraiḥ*)—that is, one distinguished by the attainment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). [He further specifies:
"of the discerning one, the dispassionate one, and the one endowed with the qualities of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth."
For it is held that only one who desires liberation possesses the fitness for the inquiry into Brahman. ||17||

The logical sequence is as follows: the fitness for the inquiry into Brahman is considered by the discerning to belong only to one who is dispassionate, endowed with qualities such as tranquility (śama), and desirous of liberation. || 17 ||

Commentary: The nature of discrimination (*viveka*) and the other [means] will be clarified later in the root text itself. The desire to know is *jijñāsā*; the desire to know Brahman is *brahmajijñāsā*. In this context, knowledge culminating in realization is the object of the desire denoted by the suffix *-san*. Consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of undivided form is the fruit of the inquiry indicated by the term *jijñāsā*. Since knowledge of Brahman in a general sense exists even prior to inquiry, if such a desired goal is to be accomplished—one must not allow even the slightest opportunity for desires and the like to arise.
One should spend the time from the moment of waking until death in reflection upon the Vedānta.

According to the manner thus stated, constant inquiry into the Vedānta is necessary. He in whom the knowledge that sublates the notion of the body as the self arises with regard to the Self alone, is liberated even against his will.
He alone is capable of producing the knowledge thus described. ||17||

The desire that gives rise to such inquiry belongs only to one endowed with the means such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest, and not to anyone else; this meaning, indicated by the word "only" (*eva*), is clarified both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the verse beginning with "the means" (*sādhanāni*). "The wise have declared four means here, in the presence of which alone there is steadfastness in the Truth, and in the absence of which it is not accomplished. (18)
In this regard, the wise have declared four means by which, when they exist, perfection is achieved; in their absence, it is not achieved. (18)
Commentary:

In the world, for whatever thing there exists either (1) the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that is co-located with what is intended as its effect, or (2) the state of having as its counter-positive an absolute non-existence co-located with what is intended as its effect, it is impossible for that thing to be the cause of that effect. For example, clay—which is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence co-located with a cloth—or which possesses a cloth that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence co-located with itself, does not attain the status of being the cause of the cloth.

Rather, the status of clay as the cause of a jar is established by virtue of grasping the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka-sahacāra)—namely, that when there is clay there is a jar, and when there is no clay there is no jar. In the same way, since the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is possible only when the fourfold means such as discrimination (*viveka*) exist—which serve as the necessary conditions for remaining firmly established in Brahman—and impossible in their absence, the understanding that these means, discrimination and the rest, are the causes of the desire to know Brahman up to its final fruit (which is synonymous with "steadfastness in them") is dependent upon the grasp of positive and negative concomitance.

Thus it has been said: "as stated by the wise. In this context, being "wise" (manīṣin) means possessing knowledge of the intended meaning of the Śruti. This is because, in the absence of reliance upon the Śruti, such qualifications of the qualified seeker are difficult to ascertain. And such wise ones are Bādarāyaṇa and others.

It is understood from the meaning of the commentary on the third section (*varṇaka*) of the first chapter (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* that those [teachers], by employing the word "then" (*atha*) within the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), were indicating the immediate succession following the attainment of the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya-sampatti*), and thus formulated the qualified seeker of the knowledge of Brahman in this manner.

However, the scriptural passages that provide such specific qualifications—such as the reasoning that "whatever is produced is impermanent," the texts stating, "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, so too there the world acquired by merit perishes," "That which is plenitude (bhūman) is immortal; other than that, everything is afflicted," and "The wise one is neither born nor dies"—are discriminative, as they teach the eternity of the Self and the non-eternity of the non-Self.

"The Brahmin, having examined the worlds acquired through action, should attain detachment, for there is nothing uncreated that can be gained by what is created"—this Śruti passage, beginning with "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband" and ending with "but for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear," establishes dispassion toward everything other than the Self. Furthermore, the Śruti passage, "Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, concentrated, and possessed of faith, one should see the Self in the Self alone," teaches the sixfold discipline beginning with tranquility (śama).

The Śruti text, "He does not return again," which declares the eternity of liberation, generates a desire for it. However, since those who maintain that the Upaniṣads are merely *arthavāda* (explanatory or glorificatory passages)—namely, the followers of Karma-mīmāṃsā—hold that these texts lack any intended meaning regarding their own subject matter, the knowledge [of such a state] is impossible. Consequently, because the knowledge that "Brahman is to be sought after" and that the qualified seeker must possess such specific attributes is difficult to attain, it is said that these [teachings] were spoken by the wise.

And thus, because the Upaniṣads establish Brahman—the supreme goal of man whose nature is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time and which is not apprehended by other means of knowledge—it is only here that their ultimate validity is possible; therefore, only one who is distinguished by discrimination and the like, as presented by those various sentences, possesses the fitness for the inquiry enjoined by such passages as "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known. Thus, everything is consistent. ||18||

Therein, he points out in sequence the discernment and other qualities mentioned in the passage beginning with "of the discerning one who is dispassionate," starting with the words "In the beginning":
"In the beginning, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities is reckoned;
immediately after that, dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter. (19)

The attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama) and the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva) are clearly enumerated as follows: first, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; immediately after that, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next; the attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility; and finally, the desire for liberation. Thus it is clearly reckoned. (19)
Commentary:

Among the [means] beginning with discrimination (*viveka*), a sequence has been adopted because each preceding one is the cause of each succeeding one. Indeed, one who knows "this is eternal" and "this is non-eternal" would become dispassionate toward the non-eternal. Therefore, since dispassion (*vairāgya*) is difficult to achieve in the absence of discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, discrimination is the cause of dispassion. Only for a person possessing dispassion do tranquility (*śānti*) and self-control (*dānti*)—consisting of the restraint of the internal and external senses—become possible.

Even there, self-restraint (*dama*) consists in the cessation of the external senses precisely for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has already ceased [its activity], because when there is no connection with the mind (*manas*), the other senses are incapable of acting. If it is asked: "Since self-restraint is established by itself once tranquility (*śama*) exists, why is it included among the category of means? [The answer is: "The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind."

Thus, according to the teaching of the *Gītā*, since tranquility (*śama*) cannot be firm in the absence of restraint over the external senses, renunciation—denoted by the term "withdrawal" (*uparama*)—belongs only to one who has conquered the senses. Only such a person possesses forbearance (*titikṣā*), which consists in enduring the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold. Only such a person possesses concentration (*samādhāna*), characterized by abiding with single-minded devotion to Brahman due to the absence of external distractions. And only one endowed with these qualities possesses faith (*śraddhā*), which is the conviction in the words of the Guru and the Vedānta texts as they are taught: "Brahman alone is real; the world is illusory."

Even within the group of six beginning with tranquility (śama), the reason for their sequential order is easily stated: such a preeminent person (puruṣadhaureya) indeed desires nothing other than liberation and cannot tolerate delay therein; thus, with the intention that he must possess an intense yearning for liberation (tīvramumukṣā), [the author] first states "the eternal and the non-eternal" (nityānitya) and so forth, and immediately thereafter, "dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter" (ihāmutraphalabhogavirāga).

By stating that dispassion (*vairāgya*) follows immediately upon discriminative discernment (*viveka*), it is effectively declared—by the principle that "that which arises immediately after something is its effect"—that dispassion is the result of discriminative discernment. The phrase "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*) is to be supplied in what follows as well: immediately after dispassion comes the attainment of tranquility (*śama*) and the other [eight limbs], and immediately after that comes the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). ||19||
He explains the stated means of proof with the words beginning "Brahman," etc.:
"The firm conviction that Brahman is real and the world is illusory is of such a nature. (20)
Thus has this discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities been described. ||201/2||
The logical sequence is as follows: the firm conviction that "Brahman is real and the world is illusory" is what is designated as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. || 20 ||
Commentary:

Even when there is the certainty that Brahman is eternal and the world is non-eternal, firm dispassion (*vairāgya*) does not arise, because even non-eternal pleasure is generally desired. When it is said that the world is illusory (*mithyā*), no one desires an illusory object; for those who desire a kingdom do not long for a kingdom seen in a dream.

Therefore, for the certain arising of dispassion (*vairāgya*), he does not say "Brahman is eternal and the world is non-eternal," but rather says "Brahman is real and the world is false. By the qualifier *viniścayaḥ*, which has the sense of "ascertainment" (*niścaya*), it is indicated that the ascertainment is not undermined by any cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*). Regarding the phrase *so 'yam*: "that" refers to what was mentioned as a qualification of the discerning person (*vivekin*) in the context of "discernment between eternal and non-eternal things"; "this" refers to what was stated at the outset as "discernment between eternal and non-eternal things. This is the meaning.

The fact that this very [knowledge] is invariably the cause of detachment from the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to both this world and the next is indicated by the prefix *sam-* in the expression "it is fully illustrated" (*samudāhṛta*). ||201/2||
Having defined discernment (*viveka*), he defines detachment (*vairāgya*):
"That detachment is the loathing [of worldly objects] which arises through seeing, hearing, and so forth. (21)
For objects of enjoyment, from the body up to Brahman, are indeed impermanent. ||211/2||

The logical sequence is as follows: that aversion (or desire for renunciation) toward the objects of enjoyment—which range from the body up to Brahman and are perceived through seeing, hearing, and so forth—as being impermanent, is indeed *vairāgya* (detachment). || 21 ||
The Commentary:

By the sight of objects of enjoyment such as the body in this life; by the hearing of objects of enjoyment such as the divine body in the next life; and by the word "etcetera," by inference from what is seen and what is heard.

Detachment (*vairāgya*) is that loathing toward all objects of enjoyment—which are impermanent and illusory, extending from one's currently experienced body up to the body of Hiraṇyagarbha, the lord of the fourteen worlds who lives for a hundred years according to Brahma-measure—characterized by the thought, "May there never be a connection with such things," and an unbearable perception of them as being like the excrement of a crow. The use of the neuter pronoun "that" (*tat*) is due to the predominance of the quality of knowledge (*vidyā*), just as in the statement, "Coldness is indeed the nature of water. [As it is said:
"That man who would not be repelled by the foul odor of his own body..."
What other cause for detachment could be taught to him?
With bulls, horses, donkeys, elephants, and buffaloes constantly being driven along,
alas, it is painful that we, emaciated by hunger and exhausted, are unable even to speak.

"Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"; "Other than the Infinite, everything is afflicted"; "When their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world"; "All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return"—these [quotations] from the seventeenth chapter of the *Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa* of the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, and those in the *Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṅgraha* beginning with "In the womb, amidst the feces and urine of his mother," describe how, upon the exhaustion of merit, those who performed meritorious deeds are cast down by the denizens of heaven with their limbs rendered feeble.
Having reflected upon those who have fallen from heaven in the form of stars, who indeed would not turn away from worldly desires?

The verses beginning with "yatrāsti loke gatitāratamyam" (where there is a gradation of states of existence in the world) are to be reflected upon in relation to the subject of dispassion (*vairāgya*). The sense is that for one who reflects—using examples such as the deer and others—upon the human body being afflicted by diseases and the like, the extreme dependence of animals and other beings characterized by muteness and so forth, the oppression of gods by *rākṣasa*s and similar entities, and the capacity of objects such as sound to produce manifold misfortunes, a sense of revulsion toward everything that is not the Self becomes easily accessible.

And this will be clarified by the author himself later on with the words, "by the five alone, beginning with sound," and so forth. Although the eternity of the fruit of ritual action (*karma-phala*) is perceived from such scriptural passages as, "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," and "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible," nevertheless, there is no fault; for, in accordance with the reasoning that "whatever is produced is impermanent" and following such scriptural texts as, "Just as here those who perform rituals [perish]," it must necessarily be admitted that the terms "immortal" (*amṛta*) and "inexhaustible" (*akṣayya*) possess a restricted meaning. For it has been said:
"The state where all elements have ceased is indeed declared to be immortality. ||211/2||
He describes the nature of tranquility (śama) as follows: "Having become detached from the multitude of sense objects by repeatedly perceiving their defects... (22).
The mind's state of being restricted to its own specific object is called tranquility (śama). ||221/2||
The repeated detachment from the multitude of sense objects through the perception of their defects, and the mind's steady abiding upon its own objective, is called tranquility (śama). || 22 ||
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states:

For a person who repeatedly perceives the defects of sense objects—such as their having a beginning and an end, their being accomplished through the expenditure of great wealth and effort, and their resulting in a state of weariness upon transformation—dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward them becomes inevitable. Thus, the perception of the defects of sense objects is the cause of dispassion. And when that dispassion exists, the mind, remaining fixed upon its own object—whether characterized by qualities (*saguṇa*) or devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)—becomes motionless and free from modification. Therefore, the author says "having become dispassionate" (*virajya*) to indicate that tranquility (*śama*), which consists in the state of the mind’s fixedness, is produced by dispassion.
In that context, because the suffix *lyap* conveys posteriority in time, it is indicated that [the state] is produced by dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 221/2 ||
He defines restraint (*dama*) as "from the objects"—that is, turning [the senses] away from their objects and establishing them within their respective sockets. (23)
The restraint of both these sets of senses is proclaimed as self-control (dama). ||23 1/2 ||
The withdrawal of both types of sense organs from their objects and their stabilization within their respective sockets is proclaimed as *dama* (self-restraint). || 23 ||
Commentary:

It has been stated that because the mind possesses the capacity for investigating objects, it becomes detached by its own nature. However, since the external organs—the instruments of cognition such as the ears and so forth, and the instruments of action such as the voice and so forth—lack that capacity by their own nature, one must turn the external organs—which are like horses—away from and divert them from the uneven paths of objects such as sound, using the mind which stands in the place of a bridle; this consists of establishing them in their respective physical sockets, such as the ear-cavity, the nose, and the mouth, thereby bringing about their cessation of activity.
That which has been celebrated as self-control (dama) consists of the restraint and so forth of the mind and other faculties; this is stated in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad:
"Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot.
Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins."
"The senses they call the horses, and their objects the paths they travel"—this is the meaning. (23½)
He describes cessation (*uparati*), which is to be accomplished through the restraint of the internal organ and the external senses, with the words "external" (*bāhya*) and so forth:
"This cessation of mental activity (*vṛtti*) from not taking external objects as its support is the highest. (24)
The non-reliance on external objects by the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) is the highest form of cessation (*uparati*). || 24 ||
Commentary:

Just as the water of a pond, having emerged through the opening of a breach in the dam, undergoes transformation into the form of fields and so forth, even so, the mind situated within, having come out through the openings of the ears and other sense organs, gives rise to a mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of transformation into the forms of objects such as sound. The sense is that when the external senses are restrained, the mind situated within does not transform into an external form. ||24||

When the mind does not take external objects as its support, then, because the duality of cold, heat, and so forth is no longer perceived, even if such experiences should occur due to the power of past karma and time, the capacity to endure them—known as *titikṣā* (forbearance)—is established. Thus he says, "endurance":
"Endurance of all sufferings without seeking remedies, free from anxiety and lamentation—that is declared to be *titikṣā*. (25)
The endurance of all sufferings, preceded by a lack of remedy and free from anxiety and lamentation—that is declared to be *titikṣā*. || 25 ||

Commentary: The remedy for sufferings such as cold and heat by means of blankets, fans, and so forth, is well-known in the world. When such means are absent, there arises the thought, "What is to be done by us wretched ones? and lamentation. [The text] excludes such a state from being the endurance that serves as a means for inquiry; rather, endurance (*titikṣā*) is that which is characterized by the absence of remedies and is free from anxiety and lamentation. This refers to the endurance of sufferings—that is, of cold, heat, and other causes of suffering.
The sense is that when the mind is accompanied by anxiety, lamentation, and the like, the possibility of inquiry is cast far away. (25)
Now, he defines faith (*śraddhā*), which is the uncommon cause for the apprehension of reality, with the words "of the scripture" (*śāstrasya*):
"The ascertainment [of truth] through the conviction that the scripture—that is, the word of the Guru—is true; that is called 'faith' by the wise, by means of which reality is apprehended. (26)
The ascertainment of truth regarding the scripture and the words of the teacher is called *śraddhā* by the virtuous; it is by means of this that reality is perceived. || 26 ||
Commentary:

Even in the world, if there is a lack of trust in the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), a person will not act in accordance with them, even in matters such as deliberation; how much less so in the case of the meaning of the scriptures, which transcends the senses? Therefore, that [faith] is the supreme cause. For it is said in the *Gītā*:
"O scorcher of foes, those men who have no faith in this dharma..."
"Without reaching Me, they return to the path of death and worldly existence.

Thus, it is only one who is tranquil (*śānta*), self-controlled (*dānta*), withdrawn from worldly activity (*uparata*), and patient (*titikṣu*) who, being instructed by the Guru and the Vedāntas that Brahman alone is the single reality, that alone you are, and everything else is false, places faith in that object, thinking, "This is exactly so. No other person lacking such means can do so; therefore, faith (*śraddhā*) is subsequently enumerated as having the words of the Guru and the Vedāntas as its object. The scripture...

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) which understands that the scripture beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the words of the Guru, and the statements following them—such as "You are not a transmigrating being, but rather the Supreme Brahman whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free; everything else is false"—are true and convey an uncontradicted meaning, there arises a firm conviction (*avadhāraṇā*); that by which the reality is perceived is called "faith" (*śraddhā*) by the wise. ||26||
