Only for one possessing such faith does meditative absorption (*samādhāna*) become perfectly accomplished; therefore, he describes absorption immediately thereafter with the word "perfectly" (*samyak*):
"The constant, perfect establishment of the intellect within the pure Brahman is called that absorption, and not the pampering of the mind. (27)
The continuous, perfect stabilization of the intellect upon the pure Brahman at all times is called "concentration" (samādhi); it is certainly not the indulgence of the mind. || 27 ||
Commentary:

Although no distinction is perceived in such a state of composure with respect to the quiescence of the mind’s fixed condition upon its own object (*svalakṣya*), nevertheless, by means of this [instruction]: "Having repeatedly become dispassionate toward sense-objects through the perception of their defects, one should attain a fixed condition upon one's own object," [it is shown that] from whatever cause the flickering and unsteady mind wanders away—*yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram*.
Restraining it from this and that, one should bring it under control within the self alone.

Thus, according to the teaching of the *Gītā*, a specific effort is required in the state of tranquility (*śama*) for the stabilization of the mind, which consists of volitions and doubts. For this very reason, the firm establishment of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is determination, within the pure Brahman "at all times" implies that, in the present context, the internal organ is described as being entirely free from volitions and doubts. It is precisely for this reason that the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) is set aside and the word "intellect" (*buddhi*), characterized by the function of discernment, is employed. Furthermore, by the phrase "in the pure Brahman," the Nirguṇa (attributeless) is meant—that which is liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

At the occasion of defining *śama* (tranquility), by the phrase "remaining fixed upon its own object," it is possible to state that even when the mind remains fixed upon the qualified (*saguṇa*) [Brahman], it possesses tranquility. *Śama* is said to be the means (*sādhana*), while *samādhāna* (concentration) is its fruit—that is to say, its full maturation.

Just as in the world, when children cry excessively, people pacify them by giving them what they desire, so too, the mind’s wandering at will along the path of sense-objects is not concentration; thus he says, "but not the indulgence of the mind" (*na tu cittasya lālanam*). Alternatively—
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths, must be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort. (1)
O best among the powerful, one should cause the mind that has entered into unwholesome states to descend into wholesome ones alone, by means of the power of one's own human effort.
The mind of a living being, like that of a child, moves from the unwholesome to the wholesome, and from that as well to the other; therefore, one should move it by force. (3)
One should nurture the child of the mind with the soothing balm of equanimity—neither too quickly nor too slowly, but gradually—with manly effort. (4)

Thus, according to the method of Vasiṣṭha, either the shaking off or the nurturing [of the mind] is required as a means for attaining tranquility (śama) and the other qualities in the preliminary stage; however, this is not the case during the state of the fruition, which is samādhi. For at that time, even without such practice, once the effort made during the period of cultivating tranquility and the rest has exhausted external latent impressions (vāsanā), it is only necessary to withdraw the mind from the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman and establish it in the unqualified (nirguṇa). ||27||

Only for one adorned with such a collection of means does the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutva) arise, and not for anyone else; thus, he now describes the state of seeking liberation: "The desire to be liberated from the bonds beginning with egoity and ending with the body—which are imagined by ignorance—through the realization of one's own true nature, is the state of seeking liberation. (28)

The desire to be liberated from the bonds beginning with the ego-sense and ending with the body—all of which are imagined by ignorance—through the realization of one's own true nature, is the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutā). || 28 ||
Commentary:
Among these— the eyes and so forth— and within the body,
the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) abides through the conceit "I am," by means of its luminous manifestation.

By the statement "that is to be known as the *ahaṅkāra*," the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) endowed with the reflection of consciousness (*citpratiphalana*) is the *ahaṅkāra*. Alternatively, the enjoyer, the individual soul (*jīva*), is the *ahaṅkāra*, which is named the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*). In the definition of its own nature—through the fragments of pleasure experienced during deep sleep—it conceives, "I am becoming happy. How could that which is named the sheath of bliss (*ānandakośa*) be the Self?

Because it has been so stated, it can be said that even for that [mind], its being imagined by ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its being a modification (*vikāra*) due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the mind (*manas*) are merely secondary (*gauṇa*). And thus, in order to liberate from—meaning to abandon and sublate—the bonds beginning with the sheath of bliss (*ānandakośa*) and ending with the sheaths of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), and food (*annamaya*), which one considers to be the Self prior to the direct realization of one's true nature, so that "I-ness" (*ahantā*) may no longer arise therein through the awakening to one's own true nature; that desire is *mumukṣutā* (the state of desiring liberation). For, in the awakening to one's own true nature...

The meaning is that, according to the Śruti passage, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?", there is an absolute cessation of bondage consisting of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), due to the non-appearance of anything whatsoever distinct from oneself. ||28||

This desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) is threefold: weak, middling, and intense. Even though liberation consists of eternal bliss, the very desire for liberation is difficult to attain for those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are permeated by worldly latent impressions (vāsanā). That [desire] which arises at the time of hearing the scriptures on the supreme self (adhyātmaśāstra) does not produce any practical effect.

When a person, having perceived the defects in worldly objects through the discrimination born immediately after hearing [the teachings], attains detachment toward them, renounces all actions according to the rules, and proceeds to approach a teacher for the sake of inquiry—at that time, the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutā*) that arose during the hearing of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) is merely temporary; being indeed called "weak," it attains the state of being "middling."

To the extent that dispassion becomes intense, the mind becomes tranquil, and one desires to attain meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and when the Guru is pleased with this [aspiration], thinking, "May this person quickly cross the ocean of worldly existence," then that person desires nothing other than liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists of eternal bliss, and cannot endure any delay therein. Thus, having become a primary candidate through an intensified desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), he quickly attains the fruit. Regarding this, he says:
"Even if it is of a mild or middling form, by means of dispassion, tranquility (*śama*), and so forth, as well as the grace of the Guru, this [desire] increases and gives birth to the fruit. (29)

The sequence is as follows: even when it is of a dull or middling form, it produces fruit; this very [wisdom], having increased through the grace of the guru, through dispassion, and through tranquility and the like, [attains its full result]. (29)
Commentary:

And thus, although the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) consists of the wish for release, it is only when that [wish] has increased that it brings forth its fruit; by this it is meant that a person must exert effort for the sake of increasing it—namely, for the sake of detachment from sense objects, the sixfold discipline beginning with tranquility (*śama*), and obtaining the grace of the Guru. ||29||

Among the fourfold means [to liberation], he states that everything exists within the second and the fourth [categories], and not otherwise: "Dispassion"—that is to say, "In him alone who possesses both dispassion and an intense desire for liberation (mumukṣutva), tranquility (śama) and the other [means] become meaningful and bear fruit. (30)
Tranquility and the other qualities would be meaningful and fruitful only for one who possesses intense detachment and the desire for liberation. || 30 ||
The commentary states:

regarding the phrase "śamādayaḥ" (tranquility and so forth) in the expression "śamādayo 'rthavantaḥ" (tranquility and so forth are meaningful), the meaning of "śamādayaḥ" is the words "śama" and so forth. The sense is that the conventional usage—that such a person possesses tranquility and the other qualities—is meaningful. This refers to one who is designated by terms such as "śāntaḥ" (peaceful) and "dāntaḥ" (self-controlled), meaning one who possesses intense dispassion (vairāgya) and intense yearning for liberation (mumukṣutā); for it is precisely this intense yearning for liberation that constitutes the fruit of tranquility and the other qualities.

If there is an intense desire for liberation (tīvramumukṣutva), then, since the fruit is not obtained without the means, the cause is inferred from the effect; thus, it is easy to state that such a person possesses tranquility and the other qualities (śamādimattva). Likewise, when intense dispassion (tīvravairāgya) is known to exist in him as the means consisting of tranquility and so forth—since the fruit is certain when the means are present—it follows that his possession of tranquility and the rest is unavoidable.

The sense is this: when the means such as tranquility (*śama*) are present, and when there is intense longing for liberation (*tīvramumukṣutva*)—which is itself beyond reproach and lies between the fruit of those means and the fruit of intense dispassion (*tīvravairāgya*) and tranquility—the terms "tranquility" and so forth are meaningful in the case of intense dispassion, while "tranquility" and so forth are fruitful in the case of intense longing for liberation; such is the distinction. Since tranquility and the other qualities residing in another's internal organ are difficult to discern, it was stated that they are to be understood through their causes and effects.

When it is asked how it is to be known that a person has himself attained tranquility and so forth, the sense is that this is known when there exists an abundant cause—namely, intense dispassion (*tīvravairāgya*)—and a distinguished result—namely, the state of intense desire for liberation (*tīvramumukṣutva*), which serves as an indicator of both the cause and the effect in oneself and in others. The sages maintain that intense dispassion toward objects of enjoyment is defined as an unbearable perception of them, like the sight of a crow’s excrement; and they say that the very perception of defects in objects of enjoyment is the repository of the intensity of dispassion.

Thus, the intensity of dispassion and its means have been described in this *Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṅgraha*. Intensity regarding the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) is simply its growth; that has already been explained [previously]. (30)
Where there is dullness regarding these two—detachment and the desire for liberation—there the appearance of tranquility and the like is merely nominal, like water in a desert. //31//
The logical sequence is as follows:
where there is a dullness of these two—dispassion and the desire for liberation—there, tranquility and the other [aids] exist merely as appearances, like water in a desert mirage. || 31 ||
Commentary:

In that person in whom there is a dullness or merely temporary nature regarding these two—dispassion and the desire for liberation—it is like water in a desert. Just as during the summer heat, when the fierce rays of the sun strike the desert land, one who is at a distance may have the illusion that "there is water there," yet there is no attainment of water, nor is there any cessation of thirst; on the contrary, for the weary traveler, going toward the water with the thought that it exists results only in increased exhaustion—so too is it when intense dispassion and the desire for liberation are absent.

The meaning is that in that state, tranquility (śama) and the rest appear as mere appearances; they are not the actual fruit of tranquility and the like, nor is he designated by other terms such as "the peaceful one" (śānta) and so forth. ||31||

Thus, having described the qualifications—discrimination and so forth—for one entitled to the inquiry into Brahman, which consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and functions to determine the purport (*tātparya*) of all the Vedāntas upon the non-dual Brahman, who is identical with the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, [the author] states devotion (*bhakti*), the direct means for the immediate realization of the Self, as being accomplished by the aforementioned inquiry:
"Among the collection of causes for liberation, devotion alone is the most weighty.
Contemplation of one's own true nature is designated as devotion. (32)

The logical sequence is as follows: among the collection of causes for liberation, devotion alone is the most preeminent; therefore, the contemplation of one's own true nature is itself designated as "devotion. || 32 ||
Commentary:

"Contemplation" (nididhyāsana) is said to be the inquiry into one's own true nature, because it is the direct means for the immediate realization (sākṣātkāra) of that very [nature]. The meaning heard through the instruction of the scripture and the teacher—that "That is the Self, Thou art That," meaning "Thou art indeed Brahman, which is Thy own true nature"—is the object of that inquiry. The continuous flow of similar cognitions (sajātīya-pratyaya), unimpeded by heterogeneous cognitions (vijātīya-pratyaya) and consisting of the deepening of that meditation (bhāvanā), is the uncommon cause for immediate realization; this is the intended sense.

The meaning is that while tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] are causes for knowledge only by way of reflection (*vicāra*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), this [devotion] is so directly. For this very reason, it has been stated that among the causal complex—that is, within the collection of means for that knowledge which is the manifestor of liberation—devotion alone is the most important, because it is the direct cause. And that causal complex consists of everything from discrimination (*viveka*) up to meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). ||32||
He states the opinion of others:
"Others have declared that devotion is the contemplation of the reality of one's own self. (321/2)
Others have declared that devotion consists in the inquiry into the true nature of one's own self. (321)

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "Investigation of one's own reality" (*svātmanaḥ tattvānusandhānam*) means the investigation of the reality (*tattva*) of one's own self, that is, the individual soul (*jīva*). Its "reality" (*tattva*) is the state of being the referent of the term *tat*, meaning the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*). The "investigation" (*anusandhāna*) of that is worshiping [the Self] as non-different [from oneself], despite the existence of an actual difference; that is to say, it is worship through the identification of "I" (*ahaṅgrahopāsana*). Others have declared that this is "devotion" (*bhakti*). By this, it is indicated that this [form of devotion], which is preceded by the cognition of difference and is of the nature of delusion, does not possess the status of primary devotion. (321/2)

He states the duty for one who has been endowed with the previously mentioned means: "Endowed with the aforementioned means and desiring to know the reality, he should approach a wise guru from whom comes liberation from bondage. (331/2)

The logical connection is as follows: one who is endowed with the aforementioned means, desiring to know the reality of the self, should approach a wise teacher from whom liberation from bondage is attained. || 33 ||

Commentary: "Endowed with the aforementioned means"—the word "person" (*pumān*) is to be supplied as the subject. This refers to one who is endowed with, or possessed of, those means such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest, which have been described as the instruments for inquiry. Desiring to know the reality (*tattva*) of the Self—that is, desiring knowledge of one's own true nature—one should approach, or seek refuge with, a teacher (*guru*). Who is he? A teacher who provides instruction. Of what kind? "Wise" (*prājña*): *prajñā* is preeminent, unsurpassed knowledge or realization, namely the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman;
it is the realization of the identity between the purified Brahman and the Self.

Because it will be stated later that "the modification which is non-conceptual and pure consciousness is called *prajñā*," one who possesses such [wisdom] is *prajña*; he himself is the *prājña*. This means "one who is established in Brahman. By this, he states the fruit for himself: from whatever kind of guru [one receives] the liberation from bondage—the specific abandonment of bondage, which is imagined through ignorance and extends from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) to the body—so by approaching such a guru, liberation in the form of the cessation of bondage is accomplished through the knowledge of one's true nature (*yāthātmya-jñāna*) arising from his instruction. This is the intended meaning. ||331/2||
He characterizes such a Guru with the words beginning "one learned in the Vedas" (śrotriya):
"One learned in the Vedas, free from vice, undisturbed by desire, who is the highest among the knowers of Brahman;
who has ceased [from worldly activity] in Brahman, is tranquil, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted. (3.41)

The logical connection is as follows: he who is learned in the Vedas, free from crookedness, unassailed by desire, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, withdrawn into Brahman, tranquil, like a fire devoid of fuel. ||34||
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states:

Because it is taught by Pāṇini that "one who has studied the *chandas* is a *śrotriya*," the meaning is "one who has studied the *Upaniṣads*. This is because only one who, having studied the *Upaniṣad*, has performed inquiry into its meaning possesses the cause for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). "Free from crookedness" (*avṛjina*) means sinless. [As it is said:
"Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed..."
Nor can one whose mind is not tranquil attain this through wisdom alone.

Thus says the Śruti. Regarding this, he states the reason: "one whose desires have been destroyed" (*akāmahata*). One who is struck by desire—that is, the longing for sense objects—is "struck by desire" (*kāmahata*), meaning one whose true nature has not been revealed. One who is not struck by desire is "one whose desires have been destroyed. He who does not know the bliss that is his own nature might, at times, even commit sin in order to attain external pleasure, thinking, "There is such a thing as external bliss. However, for this most excellent knower of Brahman, because the bliss of his own nature is being directly realized, sense objects turn away from him. As it is said: "For the embodied soul who abstains from food, [objects] turn away except for their 'rasa' (flavor/taste); but having seen the Supreme Rasa, his rasa ceases. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.2)

Thus, according to the teaching of the Gītā, the state of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahatatva*), which consists in the cessation of passion, is indeed established; therefore, freedom from sin resides in that [state], since desire alone is the cause of sin. As it is said in the Gītā: "Then, by what impelled does this man commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?"

Thus questioned by Arjuna, the Blessed One said: "This desire, this anger, born of the quality of *rajas*—know this to be the great devourer, the great sinner, the enemy here. And so forth. "Stilled in Brahman" means one whose mind has dissolved into Brahman; therefore, he is tranquil like a fire without fuel. Just as fire, in the absence of fuel, appears stilled and devoid of flames, so too is he stilled because his mental fluctuations are no longer supported by external objects; he is stilled because his consciousness is firmly established in the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman—the meaning is that he is free from all modification.

In this context, the qualifying attributes such as being a śrotriya do not function as differentiators, because in one who is the best among the knowers of Brahman, the states of not being a śrotriya, being sinful, and being overcome by desire are impossible. Rather, since it is possible for them to indicate such a teacher by virtue of their actual existence, they should be understood as constituting a definition of essential nature (svarūpalakṣaṇa). ||34½||
He is an ocean of causeless compassion, a kinsman to the virtuous who bow before him. ||35||
The lineage [is as follows]: he who is an ocean of causeless compassion, a kinsman to the virtuous and to those who bow down. ||35||

Commentary: That which has no cause is "causeless" (*ahetukī*). Such compassion (*dayā*)—meaning the desire to eliminate the suffering of others—is its "ocean," that is, its locus. The compassion of another compassionate person is dependent on seeing suffering elsewhere, because they themselves have also experienced suffering [upon witnessing it]. To exclude that [type of compassion], the term "causeless" is used. However, for this [Lord], by the power of his knowledge, there is no occurrence of suffering either from himself or from others; rather, his sole intention during the period of worldly activity (*vyutthāna*) is: "May people simply cross over the ocean of saṃsāra. This is the sense.

"Bandhuḥ" means one who removes suffering. Of whom? Of "ānamatāṃ satām"—of virtuous persons who bow down; by this, it is indicated that they teach only after having fully recognized the characteristics of a disciple. Indeed, it is heard there [in the scriptures]: "This should not be given to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who is deceitful, nor to one who is not a disciple," and so forth. And it is remembered in the Gītā: "This must never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is without devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who finds fault with Me."
This is the approach to the teacher:
having propitiated that guru with devotion, bowing low with services of humility, and having obtained his favor, one should ask him about that which is to be known by oneself. (36)
The sequence [of practice] is as follows:

having propitiated the Guru, who is like darkness [in his depth], with devotion through humble prostrations, modesty, and service; and having attained the favor of that Guru, one should inquire about that which is to be known by oneself. || 36 ||

Commentary: Devotion (*bhakti*) is affection for those worthy of worship; it is a mental quality. By means of that, one is "humble" (*prahva*), meaning characterized by physical postures that manifest it—namely, with a bowed body and palms joined in reverence (*baddhāñjalipuṭa*). "With humility and service" (*praśrayasevanaiḥ*): the meaning is "by means of both humility (*praśraya*) and services (*sevanāni*)."

In that regard, "humility" consists of modest speech; "service" includes prostrating with the eight limbs of the body, massaging his feet, carrying out his instructions, and so forth. Having propitiated and served him with such service, and having gained his favor so that he is turned toward one, one should remain in his presence according to the rules and at the appropriate time, and then ask him about that which is to be known—that which one desires to understand concerning the true nature of the Self.

By the phrase "having propitiated [the Lord] through devotion, humility, and services," the purity of the three instruments (trikaraṇa-śuddhi)—consisting of purity in mind, speech, and body—of the one who propitiates is stated. ||36||

Out of compassion, the Blessed One shows the manner of worship through verbal expression preceded by devotion to those who desire to know, from the words "O Lord, salutations to You" up to "speaking thus":
"O Lord, salutations to You, O kinsman of those who bow; O ocean of compassion, [I am] fallen into the ocean of existence."
Lift me up with your own sidelong glance,
which is straight and showered with the nectar of supreme compassion.

The sequence [of the verse]: O Lord, salutations to You, the kinsman of those who bow; O ocean of compassion, lift me up—who have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence—with Your straight glance of a loving side-long look, raining down the nectar of supreme mercy. 37.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "O Friend of the world that bows" (*natalokabandho*)—the friend of the worlds, that is, of people who have bowed, the liberator from suffering; in the vocative case, "O Friend of the world that bows. "O Lord, O Master" (*svāmin prabho*), "salutation to you" (*te tubhyaṃ namaḥ*); the remainder [of the sense] is: "let there be prostration. Since you are the liberator from the suffering of the world that bows, the intention is: "therefore, I bow to you for the sake of liberation from suffering. He states the reason for this by means of the address "O Ocean of Compassion" (*kāruṇyasindho*). This has been explained in the passage "an ocean of causeless mercy" (*ahetukadayāsindhuḥ*).

He reports his own suffering, stating that he has fallen into the ocean of existence (*bhavābdhi*); the meaning is that he has fallen into the ocean of *saṃsāra*, which is crowded with the calamities of birth, old age, and death. Now he prays for its cessation, saying, "Lift me up. The meaning is: "Make me free from the bonds of birth and so forth. Therein, he requests the means: "By the glance of Your side-long look" (*ātmīyakaṭākṣadṛṣṭyā*). The meaning is: "By the corner of Your own eye. The underlying sentiment is: "When You—whose every impurity has been shaken off by the direct realization of Brahman—cast Your purifying side-long glance, I shall be liberated from all sins and cross the ocean of *saṃsāra*."
For it has been said:
"Those whose intellect, culminating in direct experience, proceeds toward the True Being (Sat),
and who come within the range of vision of such a person, are all liberated from every sin."

By this, the manner of discipline is shown: that a disciple should not stand directly in front of the Guru. Furthermore, a full glance is nothing other than a side-long look (kaṭākṣa); thus, the underlying sentiment is also "I desire that. The sense is: "When the mind, which is immersed in the bliss of the eternally pure Brahman, falls upon me fully through the medium of its outer corners, then I shall become completely purified and liberated from suffering."

Alternatively, "with her own side-glance" means with her glance of personal favor. By the adjective "straight" (*ṛjvyā*), meaning naturally simple, the intended meaning is suggested: just as in the world one who has fallen into deep water is pulled out by grasping a straight rope or staff, so too do I emerge from the ocean of saṃsāra by grasping your long, long side-glance.

Just as rays emerge from the solar disc or a lamp, gathering together like a rope, so too do rays issue forth from the eye because it is composed of light (*tejas*). Transmitted through these [rays], they lift him up due to his being joined with a mind fixed in Brahman; this is the intended meaning. "With a shower of the nectar of supreme compassion" (*atikāruṇyasudhābhivṛṣṭyā*): "supreme compassion" (*atikāruṇya*) is extreme compassion; that itself is the "nectar" (*sudhā*), which is metaphorically designated as "nectar" because it removes all afflictions.

"Sudhā" means nectar; that vision in which there is a shower [of it] from all sides is "the shower of the nectar of extreme compassion" (*atikāruṇyasudhābhivṛṣṭi*), by means of which—that is, by the shower of the nectar of extreme compassion. It is well known that through the raining down of nectar, a person becomes free from old age, death, and so forth. It is famous in the *Rāmāyaṇa* that the monkeys who died in battle were restored to life by the shower of nectar caused by Indra.

The sense is that if such nectar possesses those qualities, then the vision of the shower of the nectar of compassion from one established in Brahman will bestow the state of being free from the limitations of old age, death, and so forth. (37)
Unable to endure any delay in his own liberation, he manifests his own intense desire for emancipation as something irresistible:
"Scorched by the forest fire of saṃsāra, which is difficult to ward off,
and tossed about by the winds of misfortune..."
Protect me, who am terrified and have come to you for refuge, from death; I know no other protector. (38)
The logical connection is as follows:

since I know no other refuge, therefore, protect me—who am scorched by the forest fire of the irresistible cycle of existence, violently shaken by the winds of misfortune, and terrified of death—and who have come to you for shelter. 38.

Commentary: Saṃsāra itself is a forest fire (*vanānala*) because, like a forest fire, it pervades everything and is the cause of suffering. It is "difficult to ward off" (*durvāra*), meaning it cannot be prevented except by the knowledge born from your excellent instruction; that is, it cannot be warded off by oneself. Furthermore, this saṃsāra-forest-fire is difficult to ward off, and one is scorched and burnt by it. It is well known that when a forest fire is accompanied by wind, its capacity to spread and cause heat is great.

Likewise, "by the winds of misfortune" means by those very misfortunes—the evils—which act as adverse winds; being "shaken," or repeatedly agitated, by them. If the wind were favorable, it might carry him elsewhere, but since the wind is adverse, it causes him to fall into fire, or casts the fire upon him. With the intention that for one scorched by such a forest fire, there may be liberation from suffering through a shower of nectar, the qualification "showered with the nectar of extreme compassion from [His] glance" was given previously.

In this context, instead of forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound, one may also say: "by means of the glance (*dṛṣṭyā karaṇena*), through the showering of the nectar of great compassion (*atikāruṇyasudhābhivṛṣṭyā sudhābhivarṣaṇena*). Thus, the syntactical connection is: "Protect me, who am scorched by the forest fire of death. And so, the prior connection is: "Lift me up with your own straight glance of side-long looks (*kaṭākṣadṛṣṭyā*). With that [glance], the subsequent connection is: "By the showering of the nectar of great compassion, protect me, who am scorched by the forest fire of *saṃsāra*, from death."

The construction in both cases is: "Protect me, who am afraid of death, who have approached you, and who have come for refuge, from death. The sense is that when self-knowledge arises through your grace, my death in the form of the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) from the body is no longer possible; for the Śruti says: "His prāṇas do not depart; they are merged right here."

Furthermore, since it has been stated, "Birth is certain for one who has died," and because the absence of birth is established when there is an absence of death, the underlying meaning is: "By your grace, may I be liberated from *saṃsāra*, which consists of the continuous flow of birth and death. He reveals his own lack of any other refuge in order to draw the Guru's attention: "Since I know no other worthy of refuge" (*śaraṇya*). That is to say, because I know of no protector other than you, he is without any other refuge; therefore, the sense is that you should not remain indifferent toward him. ||38||
With these two verses, he says that for those like you, compassion toward us is indeed sincere:
"The great ones dwell in peace;
being virtuous, they act for the welfare of the world like the spring season."
Having themselves crossed the terrifying ocean of existence, they cause other people as well to cross it without any ulterior motive. ||39||
This is the very nature of the great-souled, by their own accord, to be inclined toward dispelling the fatigue of others;
indeed, this moon itself protects the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun. (40)

The lineage consists of peaceful, great, and virtuous beings who dwell like springtime, acting for the welfare of the world; having themselves crossed the formidable ocean of existence, they ferry other people across as well, without any selfish motive. (39)

This is the very nature of the great-souled ones: that they are spontaneously inclined toward dispelling the toil of others; for instance, it is said that this moon itself protects the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun. 40.

Commentary: In the rainy season there is the affliction of rain; in summer, heat; at the beginning of autumn, there is comfort—because the final portion of the last two months [of autumn] is proclaimed to be the "fangs of Yama" (yamadaṃṣṭrā); in the cold seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, there is cold; and the spring season, a source of fragrant flowers, produces happiness for the world in its entirety. Thus it is said to be "like spring," because at that time there is an absence of rain, heat, cold, disease, and the like.

Just as that season produces only happiness, so too those who extend only happiness to the world—being peaceful, with minds free from modification, and for that very reason great; possessing the undivided direct realization of Brahman, and thus being "existent" (sat) through non-difference from such true Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture, "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—have themselves crossed over that formidable and terrifying ocean of existence (bhavārṇava), which is the sea of saṃsāra; this is the meaning: they are no longer subject to worldly rebirth.

Because they have attained all their desires, they lack any personal motive; thus, "without cause" means without a motive. The sense is that they rescue others as well—those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. How can they rescue them without a cause? For no external cause need be sought for their inherent nature.

The intention is that it is not appropriate to ask what the cause of sweetness is in sugar, because it is inherent to it. "Devoted to dispelling the fatigue of others" means: the fatigue of others is their suffering; its dispelling is its removal. The term "devoted" (*pravaṇa*) refers primarily to the state of being; thus, *pravaṇatā* means the state of being inclined, attachment, or concern. This is the very nature of the great-souled ones, occurring spontaneously.

The meaning is that in this case, such things as the instigation of another are not required. He provides an illustration for this with the words beginning "sudhāṃśu" (the nectar-rayed one). The earth—the ground—is scorched on all sides by the harsh, sharp radiance of the sun; yet the nectar-rayed moon, who is well-known and situated nearby, protects it of his own accord, uninstigated by another. The particle "kila" indicates what is commonly known. ||40||

Thus, with a humble appearance, speech conforming to that, and devotion manifested thereby, [the disciple], being distressed and having no other refuge, thinks, "This person must be protected in every way," and with this intention, he earnestly entreats the Supreme Teacher—who purifies him by turning his face toward him with side-glances raining down the nectar of gracious compassion—to grant the instruction that will release him from bondage. He does so with the words beginning with *brahmānanda*:

"Sprinkle me with the nectars of your words, which are pleasant to the ear, pure, cool, and white, infused with the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss, and poured forth from the jar of your speech."
O Lord, this [world] is scorched by the flames of the forest fire of Your misfortune;
blessed are those who have been made worthy recipients and accepted by You at the moment of Your glance. (41)

O Lord, sprinkle this one, scorched by the flames of the forest-fire of worldly suffering, with the nectar of Your words—pure, cool, white, pleasing to the ears, and poured from the jar of Your speech, which is permeated by the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss. Blessed indeed are those who have been made worthy recipients, having been accepted by You at the very moment of Your glance. 41.

Commentary: O Lord, O All-Powerful One! Those persons who have become vessels—having become the locus—for the arrival of Your glance, that is, for the arrival of Your compassionate look at that very moment; or alternatively, those who have become the vessels—the recipients—of the contact with Your eyes, Your gaze, even for a mere moment—that is to say, those who have become the targets of the fall of Your eyes for just an instant—they alone are blessed and have achieved their life's purpose. They are "accepted," meaning they have been made one's own. Such persons are truly fortunate and have fulfilled their aim.
Therefore, I too, having been most graciously favored by your glance, am most blessed; desiring to quickly cool the heat of the worldly fire, I pray thus—so he indicates.

According to the maxim, "By what can one be satiated with that which is most excellent," You have accepted me as the object of Your side-glance. "Bhavatāpa" refers to the heat of worldly existence—that is, the sorrow of *saṃsāra*—which is like a forest fire (*dāvadahana*). I am scorched by its flames, utterly consumed. This person standing before You—I am like the essence (*rasa*) of the bliss of Brahman itself, to be savored. Therefore, through [the glances] infused with the experience of That, and mixed with that realization, they are consequently purified, for they remove all impurities.

"Pure" (pavitraiḥ), because of the Smṛti text: "Indeed, nothing purifying like knowledge is found here. Like such knowledge, these sentences are pure by virtue of being instructions in the form of knowledge that removes all sins. They are "very cool" (suśītaiḥ) because they destroy internal afflictions—the miseries pertaining to the self, the divine, and the elemental. They are "white" (sitaiḥ), meaning stainless, because they lead exclusively to the path of *sattva* by turning one away from the paths of *rajas* and *tamas*.

"By those poured forth from the jar of your speech": *yuṣmadvāk* means "your speech"; that faculty of speech, or its locus, the mouth, is itself the jar (*kalaśa*) or pot; from it flow the nectars of words (*vākyāmṛta*). Therefore, "by those poured forth" (*ujjhitaiḥ*) means "emitted" (*visṛṣṭaiḥ*). "Pleasant to the ear" (*śrutisukhaiḥ*) means "bringing joy to the ears. "By the nectars of words" (*vākyāmṛtaiḥ*) means "by the words themselves which are nectars. "Sprinkle me" (*secaya mām*) means "drench me" (*siceti*). The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used here for the sake of the root meaning itself.

Purity, extreme coolness, whiteness, and being released from the jar are common to both [the nectar and] the sentences; thus, the sentences are metaphorically identified with nectar. The reason for their purity is that they are "imbued with the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss" and "delightful to hear. By this it is meant that since they produce bliss even at the time of hearing, what need is there to mention the immediate bliss that would arise if one were to gain an actual experience by contemplating their meaning? ||41||

He clarifies the fear previously mentioned in the verse beginning with "frightened and having sought refuge," for the sake of accomplishing grace upon himself suddenly. He does so by means of the words beginning with "How? [namely]:
"How may I cross this ocean of worldly existence? What is my destination, and what is the means?"
O Lord, out of compassion, know me as nothing; effect the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra for me. ||42||
The sequence of meaning:
How may I cross this ocean of existence? What is my course? What means is there? I know nothing at all; protect me out of compassion! O Lord, effect the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. 42.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "How might I cross this ocean of worldly existence, which is entangled in a manifold and irresistible web of sufferings? If I continue to behave in this very same way, what will be my fate? What shall I attain? The sense is that it is nothing but suffering in every respect. Therefore, what is the means? What is the method for crossing this ocean of worldly existence? I, for my part, do not know anything at all. Protect me; preserve me who am thus terrified. He clearly prays for protection: 'Bring about the destruction of the suffering of *saṃsāra*. The meaning is: 'Uproot the sorrow of worldly existence completely. (42)
Now, with two verses beginning with "tathā," he instructs the duty of the Guru:

"Having beheld his own refugee who speaks thus, scorched by the heat of the forest-fire of saṃsāra, the Great-Souled One should immediately grant him fearlessness with a gaze moistened by the essence of compassion. (43)

Therefore, out of compassion alone, the wise teacher should impart the instruction on reality to one who has approached him for refuge, who seeks liberation, who acts according to what has been taught, whose mind is tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint. (44)

Thus, upon seeing his own disciple—who has come for refuge and is scorched by the heat of the forest fire of saṃsāra—speaking in such a manner, the Great-Souled One (the Guru), gazing with eyes moistened by the essence of compassion, should immediately grant him fearlessness. || 43 ||

That wise one should indeed, out of compassion, impart the instruction on reality to him who has approached for refuge, who seeks liberation, who acts according to what has been taught, whose mind is tranquil, and who is endowed with calmness. 44.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states:

By the phrase "speaking thus," it is indicated that because his internal qualification can be correctly known through the activity of speech, the teachers must first ascertain the qualified seeker before performing such acts as granting freedom from fear and providing instruction.

Perceiving his own self—who had come for refuge, tormented by the heat of the forest fire of *saṃsāra*—as one who has arrived seeking protection, and gazing upon him with a vision moistened by the essence of compassion, the Great-Souled One, whose intellect is not mean, should grant immediate fearlessness (*abhaya*). By this, it is implied that those who are terrified must be liberated from their fear immediately. The underlying sense is that only when a person's fear has ceased through the gift of fearlessness does the capacity to grasp the taught meaning and so forth become possible.

It has been said that "one who is capable must not allow the fear of a frightened person to persist for a long time," and thus [the Lord] spoke "at once" (*sahasā*). Having stated that the granting of safety to the frightened must first be performed, He indicates with the words beginning "the wise one" (*vidvān*) that instruction follows subsequently, according to the disciple's capacity.

He is the wise one, the best among the knowers of Brahman, the teacher; to the seeker of liberation who has approached him in the prescribed manner—that is, who has come into his presence—and who is a virtuous doer of what is taught (sādhukārī), meaning one who correctly performs the enjoined practices. By this, his status as a disciplined person (śiṣṭatva) is expressed, for it has been said: "Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain Him through wisdom."

The sense is that the teacher must examine whether the disciple possesses Vedic learning (*śrotriyatva*), integrity (*avṛjinatva*), and freedom from desires other than the desire for liberation (*mokṣakāma*). To one whose mind is tranquil—that is, who has become detached from all objects of enjoyment from the body up to Brahman; whose mind is fixed steadily upon its own true goal (*svalakṣya*); and who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*)—meaning whose external senses are restrained—thereby the group of six qualities beginning with *śama* is indicated. These are the qualifications of the eligible seeker (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).

To him, who is adorned with a multitude of virtues such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the like, one should indeed impart the instruction on reality (*tattvopadeśa*) out of compassion—that is, with the desire to eliminate his suffering. The word "indeed" (*eva*) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*), signifying that since the teacher’s desires are already fulfilled, there can be no other longing; thus, once a qualified disciple is found, one must not remain indifferent. The sense is that when the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is bestowed upon a worthy recipient, it becomes established for the sake of gracing the world.

Thus, the fruit of the instruction is the uninterrupted lineage of the knowledge of Brahman—which removes ignorance, the cause of all misfortune—and the liberation of one's own disciple. In this regard, the composition of the treatise in the form of a dialogue between teacher and disciple serves to facilitate the ascent of reality into the intellect of the listeners. For this very reason, indeed, the Śruti also employs narratives (ākhyāyikā) here and there.
By means of this, we are able to understand effortlessly all the characteristics of the teacher, the characteristics of the disciple, the points to be questioned, and so forth. ||44||

The supremely compassionate Guru, wishing to instantly dispel the fear shown by the disciple through such words as "How may I cross this ocean of existence?", said: "Do not fear! "Do not fear, O wise one; for you there is no misfortune. There exists a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
I shall point out to you that very path by which the ascetics have gone to its further shore. (45)

The sequence of the meaning: "O wise one, do not fear; there is no destruction for you. There is a means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. I shall point out to you that very path by which the ascetics have gone to its further shore. (45)

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "O wise one (*vidvan*), do not fear; let there be no fear for you"—thus, by granting immediate fearlessness, He addresses him as "wise one" to indicate that, having cultivated discernment (*viveka*) and other qualities, one must realize that crossing over suffering is not possible without the grace of a Guru. Furthermore, He suggests: "Since you have come to Me, you surely know what ought to be known. For one such as you, who acts rightly as prescribed, there is no misfortune, according to the Smṛti: "No doer of good, my dear, ever comes to a miserable state."

Therefore, [the meaning is: "Do not fear" regarding how you might cross over or what your destination may be. Having thus consoled him by saying, "Do not fear; there is no calamity for one who seeks your welfare," he states the answer to the question, "What is the means? by saying, "There is a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. Therein, in order to generate perfect conviction, he describes that means along with its authoritative basis: "I point out—that is, I instruct—that very path by which ascetics, those diligent renunciants, have gone to the further shore, the end, of this ocean of saṃsāra. ||45||
In order to achieve intensity in the desire to hear such a path, he again points out the means in a general form: "There exists," etc.
"There exists a certain great means that destroys the fear of saṃsāra;
by means of it, having crossed the ocean of existence, you shall attain supreme bliss. (46)
There exists a certain great means that destroys the fear of saṃsāra; by means of it, having crossed the ocean of existence, you shall attain supreme bliss. || 46 ||
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*):

There exists a certain great means for destroying the fear of *saṃsāra*, which is to be accomplished through many arduous practices; by that aforementioned means, having crossed the ocean of existence—the difficult-to-traverse sea of *saṃsāra*—and having shattered the ignorance (*avidyā*) that is its root, you will attain—that is, you shall obtain—supreme bliss, which is infinite and eternal contentment. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that the disciple is completely satisfied with the thought: "It is indeed the cessation of suffering that you desire; however, by the means I am about to teach, not only will suffering be utterly ceased, but there shall also be the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassed bliss for you. ||46||
He specifies that particular means: "In the Vedānta," etc.
Through the investigation of the meaning of the Vedānta, the supreme knowledge arises;
by that, there subsequently occurs the absolute destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. (47)

The logical connection is as follows: through the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta, supreme knowledge arises; by that, one experiences the absolute destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. || 47 ||

Commentary: "Vedānta" refers to the ends of the Vedas, namely the Upaniṣads. Through the inquiry into their meaning—by means of the sixfold indicators of purport such as the introduction and conclusion—the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established; He is devoid of internal or extrinsic distinctions and is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free. Through the inquiry into Him—that is, through mental activity conducive to His ascertainment—an excellent knowledge arises: a definitive certainty (nirṇaya) that is unadulterated by doubt, misconception, or other such defects.

By that definitive realization, there occurs the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra in its ultimate sense—a destruction of suffering that is not co-temporal with the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of any suffering that has the same locus as itself; "thereafter" means immediately following that realization, or it will come to be. ||47||
Now, he states the specific causes for such a determination, beginning with the word "faith" (śraddhā).
The speech of the Śruti directly declares that faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga are the causes of liberation for one who desires release.
Or rather, for one who abides in these very [principles], there is liberation from that bondage of the body which is imagined through ignorance. 48.

The speech of the Śruti directly declares that for one seeking liberation, the causes of liberation are faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga; for it is by abiding in these alone that there is liberation for him from the bondage of the body imagined through ignorance. || 48 ||
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states:

Among these, *śraddhā* (faith) is defined as trust in the Vedānta texts, the teacher, and so forth, including trust in the scripture and the words of the teacher. *Bhakti* (devotion) is the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). *Dhyāna* (meditation) is defined by the aphorism: "Meditation is the one-pointedness of the mental state directed toward that [object]. *Samādhi* (concentration) is defined as the constant, perfect stabilization of the purified intellect upon Brahman.

Yoga is defined by the aphorism: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. In this regard, faith (*śraddhā*) is the cause in all cases. Among devotion (*bhakti*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and yoga, each subsequent one has the preceding one as its cause; for when the fluctuations of the mind have ceased through concentration (*samādhi*), there arises the practice of contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), which consists of investigating one's own true nature in accordance with what has been heard from the scriptures and the instructions of the teacher.

Alternatively, from the verbal root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking," the term *dhyāna* refers to reflection (*manana*)—which consists of contemplating through logical reasoning—as the means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of *nididhyāsana*; or it may refer to meditation on the qualified form (*saguṇa-dhyāna*), which removes all evils that obstruct knowledge. In both these cases, there certainly exists the causality of *yoga*, which consists of the cessation of the mind's external fluctuations. Alternatively, *yoga* is that by which one is joined (*yujyate*) or connected with the direct realization of the Self; thus, it is a *yoga* that is devotion (*bhakti*), or a *yoga* that is meditation (*dhyāna*). Hence, the connection is either *bhaktiyoga* or *dhyānayoga*.

For the person desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*—the sacred word of the *Śruti*—directly declares the causes of liberation, which is the cessation of bondage, in the passage: "Know [it] through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga. This means that the direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) speaks thus. Alternatively, the construction may be: the *Śruti*, containing the word "know" (*avehi*), declares the direct causes—that is, the immediate reasons—for liberation, which is the knowledge that is the cause of liberation.

"Whosoever, indeed, stands firm in these very things—faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga; he who is always full of faith, possessed of devotion, a meditator, and a yogi—for him... [the result follows].

By the use of the word *adas* (that), [the author] indicates the rarity of such qualified aspirants, since it is said that *adas* refers to what is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*). The remainder [of the meaning] is that for him, liberation—that is, cessation—from the bondage of the body, which is imagined by ignorance and rooted in nescience, namely from the bondage of the body consisting of ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, is indeed accomplished. In the phrase "or whoever" (*yo vā*), the particle *vai* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and is to be connected with the end [of the sentence]. In the phrase "in these alone," the emphasis excludes the possibility of being intent upon means other than those already mentioned. ||48||

Now, the Guru briefly instructs the disciple regarding the cause of worldly existence, its root cause, and the means for its cessation, along with their underlying reasons: "From the union with ignorance...
From the union with ignorance, indeed, there is for you the bondage of the non-Self to the Supreme Self; from that alone arises worldly existence.
The fire of wisdom arising from the discernment of those two shall burn away the effects of ignorance, root and branch. ||49||

The bondage to the non-Self is indeed due to your connection with ignorance regarding the Supreme Self; from that alone comes transmigration. May the fire of awakening, arising from the discrimination between these two, utterly consume the effects of ignorance along with their very roots. (49)
Commentary:

O Supreme Self, due to the conjunction with ignorance—that is, through the connection with beginningless avidyā—there arises the bondage of the non-Self, which is the notion of being the Self in what is not the Self, namely, in the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. From that very source proceeds saṃsāra, consisting of the superimposition (adhyāsa) of attributes such as birth, old age, death, pleasure, pain, and insentience.

The fire of discernment (*viveka*)—which is the knowledge arisen from the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self—is the fire in the form of direct realization produced by that discernment, which is the knowledge of distinction. It would burn away, completely reducing to ashes, the bondage beginning with the ego-sense and ending with the body, along with its seed in the form of ignorance and its effects, as well as the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) consisting of birth, old age, death, and so forth, which are brought about by that bondage. This is the meaning.

Thus, it has been stated in brief: the cause of transmigration is bondage to the non-Self; the cause of that is the conjunction with ignorance (*ajñāna*); the means for its cessation is the realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-bodha*); and the cause of that [realization] is the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. By this, the logical justification has been demonstrated regarding the fact that the supreme knowledge born from Vedāntic inquiry destroys the suffering of saṃsāra—namely, that bondage arising from ignorance ceases through knowledge alone and not by any other means. ||49||

Thus gladdened by the flow of the nectar of words issuing from the lotus-face of the Guru, the disciple—desiring to plunge deeply into the ocean of the ambrosia of speech pouring forth without restraint from the jar of his mouth—respectfully requests him to ask [further] in order to shatter all his doubts. The disciple said: "O Lord, please listen; this question is being asked by me."
Having heard your reply from your own lips, I shall have achieved my purpose. (50)
O Master, please listen out of compassion to this question being asked through your mouth; having heard the answer from you, I shall have attained my life's purpose. (50)
Commentary:

By this, the duty of the disciple is taught that one should not pose a question without first informing the Guru. Regarding "the answer to which is the answer": by not saying, "This question is being asked by me," but rather first making the request, "Please listen out of compassion," he indicates—through his speech—the increase of the Guru's affection for him, as well as the Guru's mental gentleness and his own state of eager desire to know. By the phrase "having heard from your mouth," it is made known that he has no other refuge. (50)

The meditation on the non-existence of objects and the state of being established as the Fourth (*turyagā*)—expressed by the term *saṃsthiti* in the phrase "liberation is abiding as the Self that is Brahman"—are indicated here by that word as signifying one’s own direct experience accompanied by the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). By this, it is also suggested that the states of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya* do not constitute primary liberation; for all four of these relate to the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman and are therefore illusory, since the nature of Brahman—which is devoid of the three types of limitation—is impossible to find in the qualified Brahman.

The connection is as follows: liberation (mukti) is indeed isolation (kaivalya), which is the state of abiding as Brahman—free from the relationship with all imagined varieties of limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—in one's own essential nature that is eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), and perfectly full; this is not obtained without the merits performed over hundreds of millions of births. ||2||
These three things are indeed difficult to obtain, being caused by the grace of the gods:
human birth, the desire for liberation, and reliance upon a Great Being. (3)
The sequence is as follows: human birth, the desire for liberation, and reliance upon a great soul—this triad, caused by divine grace, is indeed difficult to obtain. ||3||
Having somehow attained the rare birth as a human being, and therein even manhood and the mastery of the Vedas,
that person of deluded intellect who does not strive for the liberation of his own self— how can he be called wise?
He is a destroyer of himself; through his false grasping, he destroys his own self.

Having somehow obtained a human birth, which is difficult to find, and even therein manhood and the ability to see the further shore of the Vedas, that fool who does not strive for the liberation of his own self is a destroyer of himself; through his attachment to the unreal, he destroys his own soul. ||4||
Who is there more foolish than this person who, having obtained a human body so difficult to attain—and even therein the state of manhood—neglects his own true welfare? (5)
Who else here is more foolish than he who, having obtained this rare human body and even within it the power of human effort, yet remains negligent regarding his own true welfare? (5)
Let them study the scriptures, let them worship the gods, let them perform rituals, and let them revere the deities;
yet without the realization of the identity of the Self, there is no liberation.
It is not accomplished even within a hundred Brahmās. ||6||

Let them study the scriptures, let them sacrifice to the gods, let them perform rituals, and let them worship the deities; yet without the realization of the identity of the Self, liberation is not achieved even within a hundred Brahmās. (6)
For the Śruti clearly declares that there is no hope for immortality through wealth, since it explicitly states that ritual action is not the cause of liberation. ||7||
The sequence [of reasoning] is as follows: since it is clear that action is not the cause of liberation, for the Śruti indeed declares, "One does not hope for immortality through wealth. (7)

The Commentary: Since human birth, manliness, and so forth are attainable only through the excellence of merit accumulated over many births; since a person must remain vigilant regarding their own true welfare; and since liberation—which consists of the absolute cessation of suffering and unsurpassed bliss—does not manifest directly through the entire collection of ritual acts such as the study and performance of the *karmakāṇḍa* without the realization of the identity of the Self; and since the Śruti itself directly states this matter regarding actions accomplished by wealth, saying, "There is no hope for immortality through wealth."
He has directly sought the utility [of this knowledge] for liberation; therefore, "the wise man should strive for liberation"—
that is, the wise man, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects, should strive for liberation.
Having approached a peaceful and great teacher, his self became concentrated on the meaning taught by him.

Therefore, the wise person, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects, should strive for liberation; having approached a virtuous and great teacher, he should have his soul intent upon the goal taught by that teacher. (8)
Commentary:
"The wise one" is said to be one who possesses the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal.
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the sources of suffering.
O son of Kuntī, they have a beginning and an end; the wise man does not delight in them.

Thus, because this very point has been indicated by the word "wise" (*budha*) in the *Gītā*, the phrase "external objects" (*bāhyārtha*) illuminates the impermanence of sensual pleasure. Since external objects are adventitious by virtue of their being outside [the self], they lack constancy; therefore, the manifestation of pleasure produced by them is likewise characterized by that same nature. Consequently, a discerning person who is the foremost among men must abandon desire for that [pleasure]; thus, he first states the method of effort: "having become one whose longing for the pleasure of external objects has been renounced."

"External" (bāhya) and "objects" (artha) constitute "external objects" (bāhyārtha). Pleasure derived from those is "pleasure in external objects" (bāhyārthasukha). Longing for that is "longing for pleasure in external objects" (bāhyārthasukhaspṛhā). He by whom this has been renounced is described as one who is dispassionate toward the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to both this world and the next. By this, it is essentially stated that his inner self (svānta) has been rendered utterly pure through the desireless performance of actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.

The phrase "He who exists" (san) indicates that for one who lacks discrimination and is greedy for sense-objects, even mere existence is difficult to attain. According to the Śruti: "A man who has a teacher knows," and "From the teacher alone is knowledge obtained; from him one reaches the highest good. Since the identity with the Self, which transcends the senses, cannot be realized without a Guru, it is said—by the words beginning with "He who exists"—that one must take refuge in a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) in the manner previously described. The meaning of "san" is "he who exists" (asti).

"If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existent. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. "That which is the Plenum (bhūmā), that is the Immortal; everything other than that is afflicted. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.
"The existence of the non-existent is not found; the non-existence of the existent is not found.
The limit of both has been perceived by the seers of reality."

Because existence (*astitva*), characterized by being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, belongs to Brahman alone according to such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as these; and because the Guru possesses that same nature due to his non-difference from Him, as stated in the scripture, "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself. By this, the steadfastness in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*), which consists in the complete cessation of identification with unreal, non-self entities, is indicated.

"Desiring to know That, one should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman"; and from such scriptural passages as, "There is no path here for one who has not been instructed by another; for [the Truth] is subtler than the subtlest, beyond mere reasoning. For it is only from such a Guru that the pure knowledge of the Self—free from doubt, mental impressions, and the like—is possible.

This is indeed logical: even in the world, a path never before seen by us must surely be pointed out by those who have already seen that path; and even if something is somehow discovered by oneself, any doubt regarding it must surely be dispelled by those who have perceived its true nature.

In this regard, the dialogue between Śuka and Janaka serves as authoritative evidence. For it is recorded in the *Vāsiṣṭha* and other texts that although Śuka had himself realized the objects of knowledge through the ripening of merits performed in previous births, he nevertheless attained rest in Brahman with his mind settled there at the word of his father, the great-souled Janaka of Videha, even though he had already been instructed by him. Thus, because he is non-different from Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sat*), the Guru possesses the nature of Being. For this very reason, he possesses greatness. Because he has discerned the five sheaths (*kośa*), he is unlimited.
Alternatively, he is adorned with all the excellent qualities mentioned in the scriptures. As will be stated:
He is a master of the Vedas, free from vice, and untainted by desire; he is the supreme knower of Brahman, an ocean of causeless compassion, and a kinsman to the virtuous who bow before him.
"Resting in Brahman, tranquil, like a fire without fuel"—such is the collection of qualities [described].

He is a *deśika* (guide) because he imparts knowledge to his disciples; having approached him according to the prescribed rule (*yathāvidhi*) and having attended upon him, one whose self—that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is properly fixed upon that very object taught by that Guru, which consists of the nature of Brahman as well as the means for attaining it, should strive for liberation. By the phrase "should strive for liberation," the state of being a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣutva*) is implied, since effort toward that end is impossible without the desire for liberation.

By the phrase "with the self concentrated on the taught object," it is stated that since a mind constantly concentrated on Brahman is impossible without the renunciation of all actions, a person of discrimination who possesses dispassion must, by his very nature, first renounce all actions and, having approached a Guru established in Brahman, engage in the inquiry into Brahman at all times. ||8||

He explains the meaning briefly stated [in the previous verse] with seven verses. Therein, since the effort exerted for the sake of liberation culminates in the perfection of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), he describes—in this verse—the perfection of right vision as the direct means to liberation and the primary cause therein, namely the state of being "ascended in yoga" (*yogārūḍhatva*), which is synonymous with supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*): "Having attained the state of being ascended in yoga through steadfastness in right vision, one should uplift oneself by means of the self, when it has sunk into the ocean of worldly existence. (9)

The logical sequence is as follows: having attained the state of being established in yoga, one should, through steadfastness in right vision, uplift by means of the self the very self that has been submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. ||9||
The Commentary:
When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitional constructions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.
Thus, according to the word of the Blessed One,
the meaning is that steadfastness in right vision preceded by supreme detachment alone is the cause for uplifting the self fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra.
[It is] joined with the waves of the fivefold afflictions and the like, and abounding in delusion.

Having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra— filled with the fish of wives, sons, acquired wealth, and kinsmen, and possessing the mass of passion born of the god of love that resembles the submarine fire— I go unto Hari.

O Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, grant me the support of Your hand to me— who am like one being seized and restrained by the vast, terrifying crocodiles and sea-monsters of Time in the ocean of saṃsāra, and who am distressed by the sharks of the multitude of passions.

In this manner, because saṃsāra—which consists of ignorance and its manifestations—is difficult to cross without perfect knowledge, it is metaphorically described as an ocean. For one who regards the non-self body as the self, it is impossible to realize that when the body is born or dies, its attributes do not belong to oneself; nor can one realize this regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) when it is afflicted by hunger and thirst, or regarding the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) when it is experiencing pleasure or pain.

Thus, because ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*) are continuous, the pentad of afflictions and so forth is described as having the nature of waves. "Error is indeed error"; "the notion of something in what is not that" is the whirlpool, and so on, is clear. Due to beginningless ignorance, the ignorant person—thinking "I am an agent," "I am a human being," and so forth—remains in the gross, subtle, and causal bodies which are not the Self. This state of non-attainment of one's true nature is itself immersion in the ocean of *saṃsāra* for the Self, whose nature is unattached, pure consciousness, and bliss. Even there, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*)...

Since saṃsāra is not experienced [by the Self], it must be stated that its very root lies in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the form of the mind of one who lacks discrimination. For it is heard in scripture:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense-objects, it leads to bondage; free from objects, it is known as the means to liberation."
Therefore, it is due to the mind being devoid of discernment that it becomes attached to the body and so forth, while the Self remains submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.

Therefore, when the mind becomes refined by the purificatory impressions (*saṃskāra*) derived from scriptural study, reflection, and so forth, it then becomes free from delusion through the attainment of knowledge of the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya-jñāna*). One should uplift the undiscriminating mind—that is, one should withdraw it from non-Self objects—by means of a mind possessed of discrimination born of scripture. Thus, because of its inherent tendency toward extroversion, the mind is attached to external things such as the body; and although the Self is in reality unattached, it appears as if attached, like a crystal appearing red due to proximity with a red object. It is for this [Self] that [the mind must be withdrawn].

The sense is that when there is an absence of connection with the non-self due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and when one is established solely in the Self by being turned inward, the Self becomes as if uplifted.

The syntactical connection is: having attained the state of being established in yoga, one should uplift the self—which is submerged in the ocean of worldly existence—by means of the Self through steadfastness in right vision. ||9||

Clarifying the state of being established in yoga, he first describes hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption—which follow renunciation—as the means for attaining steadfastness in right vision, beginning with the words "having renounced":
"Having renounced all actions for the sake of liberation from the bondage of worldly existence, let the wise and steadfast ones, intent upon the practice of the Self, strive. (10)
The wise and steadfast, having approached and renounced all actions for the sake of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence, should strive in the practice of the Self. 10.
The Commentary:

Having renounced all actions—that is, having abandoned even by their very nature those things prescribed in the *Karmakāṇḍa*—for the sake of liberation from the bondage of existence (*bhava-bandha*), which is to say, for the sake of steadfastness in right vision (*samyag-darśana*) that serves as the cause for the cessation of worldly bondage; [this was taught] by the "wise" (*paṇḍitaḥ*), meaning those possessing indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) regarding the Self, and by the "steadfast" (*dhīraḥ*), meaning those who have mastered their intellects. [As it is said:
"The Self-existent One pierced the openings directed outward."
Therefore, one looks outward and not at the inner self;
yet some wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inward self with his gaze turned back.

Thus says the Śruti. One who bestows wisdom (*dhi*) is called *dhīra*; when it is said that he brings the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is the primary element among the aggregate of causes and effects—under his control, the conquest of the other senses is established as a matter of course. By this, his possession of tranquility and other qualities is indicated.
For this very reason, regarding the practice of the Self: "Meditating upon That, speaking of That, and mutually awakening one another to That."
And the wise know that single-minded devotion to this is the practice of Brahman.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by those who are present—that is, engaged—in the activities described in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, which consist of reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard, explaining it, and mutually awakening one another according to the saying of the learned; let them strive through the practice of *nididhyāsana*, which is a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīyapratyaya*) unobstructed by heterogeneous impressions (*vijātīyapratyaya*). For such a person, the state of being "established in yoga" (*yogārūḍhatva*), synonymous with supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*), should be understood as already accomplished through the renunciation of all volitional constructions (*sarvasaṅkalpasaṃnyāsa*). ||10||

If it be objected that, since the scriptures enjoin the performance of action throughout one's entire life—such as "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa rites as long as one lives," "One should worship the twilight devotions day by day," and "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years"—it would follow that renouncing all actions constitutes a transgression of the scriptures, we reply: no, because those scriptural passages have as their subject matter those whose minds are not yet purified.

For this very reason, the *Īśāvāsya* mantra states: "Thus [it is] for you, and not otherwise; there is no other path than this by which action does not cling to a man. This means that for you—a man who identifies as a mere human—there exists no other way, distinct from the performance of action, that serves as the cause for the non-clinging of action. [As it is said: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality; the self-controlled ones, whose nature is purified through the yoga of renunciation."
For these eighteen forms of sacrifice, which consist of ritual action, are said to be inferior and unstable rafts;
those fools who rejoice in this [path] as the highest good, [are deluded].
They return once again to old age and death.

For it has been prescribed that there is renunciation of action through such statements as, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? and because action itself has been censured.

By reflecting on the meaning of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self," it is determined that these [rites] serve as means to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) by way of the purification of the mind, but not that they must be performed at all times.

If that were the case, it would result in a contradiction of scriptural injunctions prescribing renunciation, such as, "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," as well as the inconsistency of the censure of ritual action (*karman*). For this very reason, the same point is stated by the two *sūtras*: "Therefore, there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires, etc. and "There is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifices and so forth, as in the case of the horse.
