Ritual actions do not have liberation—the supreme human goal—as their direct purpose; rather, they serve as an external auxiliary to knowledge by way of purifying the mind. This is what he expresses with the words beginning with "of the mind": ... [the text continues] ... [The passage concludes: ... "The mind is purified by the practice of the duties of one's own station (*svadharma*); when the mind is purified, knowledge arises from that [purification]. Thus, the meaning is that the purification of the mind is the immediate cause for the arising of knowledge, while the duties of one’s own station are the remote cause. Therefore, the statement that "one should abandon all duties" is intended to mean that one should abandon those duties other than the practice of one’s own station, which is the means to the purification of the mind. Otherwise, since the abandonment of all duties is impossible, it would follow that even the duties of one’s own station must be abandoned. Furthermore, the following objection might arise: "If the duties of one’s own station are indeed the means to the purification of the mind, then why is it said that 'one should abandon all duties'? To this, he replies: "This is said with reference to the duties of others. The meaning is that the abandonment of all duties is enjoined with respect to duties other than those of one’s own station. This is because the abandonment of duties other than one’s own station is possible, whereas the abandonment of one’s own station is impossible. Moreover, the abandonment of all duties is enjoined for one who has attained knowledge, because for such a person, duties other than those of one’s own station are no longer required. However, for one who has not yet attained knowledge, the abandonment of all duties is not enjoined, because for such a person, the duties of one’s own station are still necessary. Thus, the abandonment of all duties is enjoined only with reference to duties other than those of one’s own station. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the following might be asked: "If the duties of one’s own station are the means to the purification of the mind, then how can it be said that 'one should abandon all duties'? To this, he replies: "This is said with reference to the duties of others. The meaning is that the abandonment of all duties is enjoined with respect to duties other than those of one’s own station. This is because the abandonment of duties other than one’s own station is possible, whereas the abandonment of one’s own station is impossible. Having renounced all actions prescribed in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and having abandoned them even in their essential nature, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of existence—that is, for the sake of steadfastness in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the cause for the cessation of worldly bondage—one should act with the wise (*paṇḍitaḥ*), who possess indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) concerning the Self, and with the steadfast (*dhīraḥ*), whose intellects are self-controlled. For it is said:
"The Self-existent One pierced the openings [of the senses] outward;
therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self."

"A certain wise person (dhīra) beheld the inner Self, with eyes turned inward, desiring immortality"—so says the Śruti. One who bestows intelligence (dhiyam rāti) is "wise" (dhīra); when it is said that he brings the intellect (buddhi)—which is the primary element among the aggregate of causes and effects—under his control, the conquest of the other senses is established as a matter of course. By this, it is indicated that he is endowed with tranquility and other such qualities.
Therefore, regarding the practice of the Self— contemplating it, speaking of it, mutually awakening one another to it,
and being solely intent upon this— the wise know this to be the practice of Brahman.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by those who are present—that is, engaged in the activities described in the *Jñānakāṇḍa* consisting of reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard (*śruta-artha-manana*), explaining it, and mutually awakening one another—according to the manner of the statement of the learned (*abhiyukta-ukti*), let them strive through the practice of *nididhyāsana*, which consists of a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya*) unobstructed by heterogeneous impressions (*vijātīya-pratyaya*). For such a person, it should be understood that the state of being "established in yoga" (*yogārūḍhatva*), synonymous with supreme dispassion (*para-vairāgya*), is already accomplished through the renunciation of all volitional constructions (*sarva-saṅkalpa-saṃnyāsa*). ||10||

If it be objected that, because such scriptural injunctions as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives," "One should worship the twilight [Sandhyā] daily," and "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years," enjoin action throughout one's entire life, it would follow that renouncing all actions constitutes a transgression of the scriptures—[we reply: no, for those scriptures have as their subject matter those whose minds are not yet purified.

For this very reason, the *Īśāvāsya* mantra states: "Thus for you, there is no other way; action does not cling to the man. This means that for "you"—that is, for one who identifies as a mere human being—there is no other path than this performance of action that serves to prevent the clinging of karma. [As it is said: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality; the self-controlled ones, whose nature is purified through the yoga of renunciation."
For these eighteen forms of sacrifice, in which ritual action is said to be inferior, are but frail rafts. Fools are they who rejoice in this as the highest good.
They return once again to old age and death.

Because the renunciation of action is also enjoined by such passages as, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? and because action is censured [in other contexts].

By reflecting on the meaning of such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," and "Yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self," it is determined that these [actions] serve as means to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) by way of purifying the mind, but not that they must be performed at all times.

If that were the case, it would result in a contradiction with scriptural injunctions prescribing renunciation, such as, "On the very day one becomes detached, on that very day one should renounce," as well as the incongruity of the censure of ritual action (*karman*). For this very reason, this same point is stated in the two sūtras: "And therefore there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires, etc. and "There is dependence on all [actions], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Ritual actions do not serve the purpose of liberation, which is the supreme human goal; rather, they are auxiliary to knowledge by way of purifying the mind. This is what he says: "For the purification of the mind..."—ritual action is for the purification of the mind, but not for the apprehension of reality.
The establishment of reality occurs through investigation; it cannot be achieved by millions of ritual acts.
Practice is for the purification of the mind, not for the apprehension of an object; the establishment of an object occurs through investigation, not by millions of practices. (11)
The meaning is clear. He clarifies that investigation is the cause for the apprehension of the reality of an object by means of an illustration, beginning with the word "properly" (*samyak*):
"Through proper investigation, the ascertainment of the true nature of the rope is established."
She destroys the suffering of existence caused by the great serpent arisen from delusion. ||12||
The ascertainment of the reality of the rope, established through correct inquiry, destroys the suffering born of the fear of a great serpent produced by delusion. 12.
The Commentary states:

It is well known that a person who, in dim darkness, mistaking a rope fallen on the ground for a snake, becomes afraid, abandons the suffering of fear, trembling, and so forth, upon bringing a lamp and correctly investigating until he realizes the true nature of the object. In that case, the "great snake" which arose through delusion regarding the rope—the suffering produced by that [delusory] cognition—is destroyed by the ascertainment of the true nature of the rope, which is produced by correct investigation.

In the same way, the suffering of existence—the suffering produced by birth and death—which has arisen through delusion, is destroyed by the ascertainment of reality brought about by right inquiry; this ascertainment of the true nature of the self is the direct realization of Brahman. Thus, this illustration is applicable to the subject at hand in every respect. ||12||

He states that only an investigation conducted in accordance with the words of a reliable authority (āpta) is the cause for the ascertainment of an object, and no other action; thus he says: "of the object.
The ascertainment of an object is seen to result from an investigation based on beneficial instruction.
Neither by bathing, nor by giving gifts, nor even by a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). ||13||

The determination of the truth is seen to arise from beneficial instruction and inquiry; it does not arise through ritual bathing, nor through charity, nor even through hundreds of breath-restraints. || 13 ||
Commentary:

For a person who is himself deluded due to the defect of ignorance, since it is difficult for him to engage in inquiry on his own while experiencing misfortunes such as fear and trembling in the absence of any support in the form of the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*), the words of one who is beneficial are made the cause for inquiry. And "beneficiality" consists in being a speaker of things as they truly are.

The point is this: if a deluded person, instead of engaging in inquiry according to the instructions for one's welfare, performs such acts as bathing, giving gifts, or a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), then—since there is an absence of immediate valid knowledge (*aparokṣapramā*) that removes delusion—the delusion which causes misfortune will not cease; how, then, could he be one whose misfortunes have been removed? Furthermore, "inquiry" (*vicāra*) is a mental activity conducive to the ascertainment of the true nature of reality.

And likewise, it is established by perception in cases of error that it is precisely inquiry assisted by beneficial instruction that serves as the cause for the valid cognition of an object. This being so, even in the present context, the instruction is that one should effect inquiry into the Self in accordance with the teachings of the Śruti and the Guru, realize its true nature through direct intuition, and thereby liberate the Self from saṃsāra, which consists in the superimposition of the non-Self. 13.

Since only one who is capable of a particular action can possibly be the enjoyer of the fruit of that action, whereas for one who lacks such capacity it is impossible, [the author] states that external factors such as place and time possess only the status of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), while internal capacity alone is the bestower of the fruit—namely, "the qualified person" (*adhikāriṇam*).
"The success of the fruit especially awaits the qualified person;
means such as place and time are its auxiliaries in this regard. (14)

The logical connection is as follows: in this [sacrifice], the attainment of the fruit depends specifically upon place, time, and so forth; furthermore, there exist the qualified agent, the means, and the auxiliary factors. 14.
Commentary:

Since ritual actions (*karma*) have visible purposes, one must accept that place and time are also specific causes, in accordance with scriptural injunctions such as: "One offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," "One offers in the footprint of the horse," "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east," "One offers in the evening," "One offers in the morning," "One should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma* every spring," and "In spring, one should establish the sacred fires. This is true even though [place and time] are also [factors] for knowledge.
As it is in a mirror, so it is in the self; as it is in a dream, so it is in the world of the ancestors;
as one sees [a reflection] as if in water, so it is in the world of the Gandharvas; and as in shadow and light, so it is in the world of Brahmā.

"In this world, if one has known [the Self], then there is truth; if one has not known it here, there is great ruin"—according to such scriptural passages, it is understood that only the world of humans and the world of Brahmā constitute the ground for knowledge. Thus...
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
for he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes to perdition.

According to such authoritative texts as, "Having completed the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (vanī) and then renounce," it appears that even the time for renunciation—which is an internal means to the knowledge of Brahman—is being prescribed. Nevertheless, Virocana, the king of the Rākṣasas, whose mind was impure, did not grasp the Self even after going to the world of Brahmā and being instructed by the Supreme Guru, Parameṣṭhin. For it is said: "Those who have attained supreme detachment renounce the world without having married, having perceived the world of transmigration itself to be essence-less and desiring to see the true essence."

By such scriptural authorities as, "Or else, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), or from the householder's life, or from the forest; on whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," the intention is that for one who is endowed with the fourfold means—beginning with the aforementioned detachment—neither place nor time is intended [as restrictive factors]; thus, their status as auxiliary factors has been stated.

For this very reason, in the passage, "The wise man, having renounced the desire for the pleasure of external objects," the two factors of discrimination (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) are established as the causes for the concentration of the mind upon the meaning taught by a Guru—preceded by approaching such a Guru who instructs in the means to liberation—for the sake of steadfastness in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the direct cause of liberation characterized by abiding as Brahman-Ātman.

Since such concentration of the mind is impossible in the absence of tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), withdrawal (*uparati*), forbearance (*titikṣā*), and faith (*śraddhā*), and since effort for that purpose is impossible in the absence of a desire for liberation, the first verse beginning with "Therefore, for the sake of liberation" has indeed indicated the common causes for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*): discrimination (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), the sixfold set beginning with tranquility (*śamādi-ṣaṭka*), and the state of being a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣutva*).

And thus, in accordance with such scriptural passages as "He crosses over sorrow" (*tarati śokam ātmavit*) and "For the sake of knowing That, one should approach a guru alone," right knowledge—which destroys the bondage denoted by the word "sorrow"—cannot be attained by any other means whatsoever without the investigation of the subject matter taught by a true guru. In this verse, the word *asyām* (in this) has the meaning of *siddhau* (in the accomplishment). ||14||
Therefore, having approached a teacher who is an ocean of compassion and the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, the seeker of the reality of the Self must engage in inquiry. (15)

The logical sequence is as follows: therefore, having approached a Guru who is an ocean of compassion and the highest among the knowers of Brahman, one who desires to know must undertake an inquiry into the reality of the Self. ||15||
Commentary:

Therefore, because it is the cause for the definitive resolution that removes all misfortunes, the inquiry into the reality of the Self must be undertaken by a person desiring to know the Self correctly—that is, one who desires to know the Self well. Regarding this, he states the procedure to be followed: [one should approach] the "Ocean of Compassion. By virtue of having achieved his own purpose, the Master's lack of personal need is already established; yet, out of compassion—meaning an ocean of pity—thinking, "May others also not experience suffering," he is like a mass of water for waters. [He approaches] the "Guru": the syllable *gu* refers to darkness (*andhakāra*), and the syllable *ru* refers to its obstructer.
Because he brings about the cessation of darkness, he is called "the Guru."

Thus, according to the manner stated by the Guru-gītā, the meaning is that [the teaching] removes the internal darkness known as ignorance (*ajñāna*) through its own instruction. Just as darkness, having enveloped the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), becomes an obstacle to the knowledge of it, so too ignorance, having enveloped the Self (*ātman*), becomes an obstacle to its clear manifestation; such is the "darkness-nature" of ignorance. For this very reason, it is designated by words such as "darkness" (*tamas*) in the Śruti, as in passages such as: "Darkness indeed existed, hidden by darkness in the beginning."

He describes that person in whom these two qualifications are possible as "the best among the knowers of Brahman" (*brahmaviduttama*). Those who know Brahman are the "knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*); the meaning is "the best among them," namely the one whose wisdom is firmly established (*sthitaprajña*). Regarding this, the scriptural citations have been quoted previously.
And the means for attaining him is stated thus: "Having propitiated that Guru with devotion, bowing low with services of humility," according to the method that will be explained hereafter.

"And know that [the Guru] by prostration, by inquiry, and by service"—according to this teaching of the *Gītā*, one brings him face-to-face with one's own Self. Thus, the explanation of the eighth verse, beginning with "for the sake of liberation," has been completed by these many verses. ||15||
A wise and learned man, skilled in the processes of reasoning and refutation, and characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self. ||16||
The logical connection is as follows:
a learned and intelligent person, skilled in reasoning through inquiry and refutation, who is characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is qualified for the knowledge of the Self. 16.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*):

It was stated that "the accomplishment of the fruit especially awaits the qualified person" (*adhikārin*); now, with the words beginning "the wise one" (*medhāvī*), he describes that qualified person in the present context.

From the *Kośa* [Amarakośa], which states "medhā is wisdom endowed with retentive power (*dhāraṇāvatī*)," one who possesses an intellect capable of retaining the meaning of what has been heard is called *medhāvī*; by the etymological derivation "one who has *medhā*," the word *medhāvī* refers to a learned person. One who has studied poetry, lexicons, and grammar is so described. By the phrase "skilled in reasoning and refutation" (*ūhāpohavicakṣaṇaḥ*), it is understood that his intellect is refined by logic (*tarka*) and hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*).

"One who knows words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge" (padavākyapramāṇajña) means one characterized by the definitions stated [previously]. This refers to one endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhana*)—discrimination, dispassion, the six qualities beginning with tranquility (*śama*), and the desire for liberation—as indicated through both concise and detailed explanations in the verses occurring from the eighth up to the fifteenth verse. Such a person is qualified for the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) and is fit to experience liberation, which is the fruit of that science. ||16||

The characteristics have been stated clearly for the sake of easy comprehension; having encompassed them, he says "for the discerning one. Alternatively, the characteristic mentioned is the state of being desirous of knowledge (*jijñāsutva*).

Regarding the statement, "The seeker of the reality of the Self (ātma-vastu) must practice non-discursive inquiry (avicāra)," it is the seeker alone—distinguished by qualities such as intelligence—who partakes in the fruit of the knowledge of the Self. If one asks, "Who now has the qualification for this inquiry? [the author] says "of the discerning one" (vivekinaḥ), referring to the person characterized by the attainment of the fourfold means (sādhana-catuṣṭaya), who was indicated by the word "by the wise" (dhīraiḥ) in the tenth verse, and described in the eighth verse as "the learned one who has abandoned the desire for the pleasure of external objects, with his mind concentrated on the taught meaning. Thus: "of the discerning one"—that is, of one who is dispassionate and endowed with the virtues of tranquility (śama) and so forth.
For it is held that only one who desires liberation possesses the fitness for the inquiry into Brahman. ||17||

The logical sequence is as follows: fitness for the inquiry into Brahman is considered by the discerning to belong only to one who is dispassionate, endowed with qualities such as tranquility, and desirous of liberation. || 17 ||
Commentary:

The nature of *viveka* (discrimination) and the other means will be clarified later in the root text itself. The desire to know is *jijñāsā*; thus, "the desire to know Brahman" is *brahmajijñāsā*. In this context, knowledge culminating in realization (*avagati*) is the object of the desire denoted by the suffix *-san*. Consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of undivided form is the fruit of the inquiry indicated by the term *jijñāsā*. Since a general knowledge of Brahman exists even prior to inquiry, if such a desired goal is to be accomplished—one must not allow even the slightest opportunity for desires and the like to arise.
One should spend the time from the moment of waking until death in contemplation on the Vedānta.

According to the method thus stated, constant inquiry into the Vedānta is necessary. He in whom the knowledge that sublates the notion of the body as the self arises with regard to the Self alone, is liberated even against his will.
He alone is capable of generating the knowledge thus described. ||17||

He clarifies, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*), the meaning indicated by the word "only" (*eva*)—namely, that the fitness for such a desire that generates this kind of inquiry belongs only to one endowed with the means such as discrimination (*viveka*), and not to anyone else—by stating: "The means...
"The wise have declared four means here;
when these alone exist, there is steadfastness in the Truth, which is not accomplished in their absence. (18)
In this regard, the wise have declared four means by which, when present, perfection is achieved, but in whose absence it is not achieved. (18)
Commentary:

In the world, for whatever thing there exists either (1) the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that is co-located with what is intended as its effect, or (2) the state of having as its counter-positive an absolute non-existence co-located with what is intended as its effect, it is impossible for that thing to possess causality toward that effect. For example, clay—which is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence co-located with a cloth—or which possesses a cloth that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence co-located with itself, does not attain the status of being the cause of the cloth.

Rather, the status of clay as the cause of a jar is established by virtue of grasping the concomitance of presence and absence—namely, that when there is clay there is a jar, and when there is no clay there is no jar. Similarly, since the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is possible only when the fourfold means such as discrimination (*viveka*) exist—and impossible in their absence—the understanding that these means (discrimination and so forth) are the causes of the desire to know Brahman, which culminates in its fruit and is synonymous with steadfastness in Brahman, depends upon the grasp of the concomitance of presence and absence.

Thus it has been said: "spoken by the wise. In this context, being "wise" (manīṣitva) consists in possessing knowledge of the intended meaning of the Śruti. This is because such qualifications of the qualified seeker are difficult to ascertain in the absence of reliance upon the Śruti. And such wise ones are Bādarāyaṇa and others.

It is understood from the meaning of the commentary on the third section (*varṇaka*) of the first chapter (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* that those [teachers], by means of the word "then" (*atha*) contained in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), were formulating the qualification of the seeker of Brahman as being one who possesses the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya-sampatti*) immediately preceding that inquiry.

However, those scriptural passages that provide such specific qualifications—such as the reasoning "whatever is created is impermanent," the texts "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so the world acquired through merit perishes there," "That which is plenitude (bhūman) is immortal; everything else is afflicted," and "The wise one is neither born nor dies"—are discriminative, as they teach the permanence of the Self and the impermanence of the non-Self.

"Having examined the worlds acquired through action, a Brahmin should attain detachment, for there is nothing uncreated that can be gained by what is created"; and the Śruti beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband" and ending with "but for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear," teaches detachment from everything other than the Self. Furthermore, the Śruti—"Being calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, composed, and rich in faith, one should see the Self in the very Self"—enjoins the sixfold discipline beginning with tranquility (śama).

The Śruti text, "He does not return again," which declares the eternity of liberation, generates a desire for it. However, in the view of the Karma-mīmāṃsakas—who maintain that the Upaniṣads are merely *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory passages) and thus lack any intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding their own literal sense—such knowledge cannot possibly arise. Consequently, because the knowledge that "Brahman is to be sought after" and that there exists an eligible candidate (*adhikārī*) characterized by such qualifications is difficult to attain, it is said [in the verse] that these [qualifications] have been stated by the wise.

And thus, because the Upaniṣads establish Brahman—the Supreme Goal whose nature is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time and which is not apprehended by other means of valid knowledge—it is only here that their ultimate validity is possible; therefore, it is entirely consistent that the fitness for the inquiry enjoined by such sentences as "He is to be sought, He is to be known" belongs only to one who is distinguished by discrimination and the other means [of qualification] presented by those respective passages. ||18||

Therein, he points out in sequence the discernment and other qualities mentioned in the passage beginning with "of the discerning one who is dispassionate," starting with the words "In the beginning":
"In the beginning, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities is reckoned;
immediately after that, dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter. (19)

The attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama) and the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva) are clearly enumerated as follows: first, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; immediately after that, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next; then the attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility; and finally, the desire for liberation. Thus it is clearly reckoned. (19)

Commentary: Among the [means] beginning with discrimination (*viveka*), the sequence is adopted because each preceding one is the cause of each succeeding one. Indeed, one who knows "this is eternal" and "this is non-eternal" would become detached from the non-eternal. Therefore, in the absence of discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, detachment (*vairāgya*) is difficult to achieve; thus, discrimination is the cause of detachment. Only for a person possessing detachment do there exist tranquility (*śānti*) and self-control (*dānti*), which consist of the restraint of the internal and external senses.

Even in that case, self-restraint (*dama*) consists in the cessation of the external senses only for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has already been stilled; for when there is no connection with the mind, the other senses are incapable of acting. If it is asked, "Since self-restraint is established by itself once tranquility (*śama*) exists, why is it included among the category of means? [the answer is: "The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind."

Thus, according to the manner stated in the *Gītā*, since tranquility (*śama*) cannot be firm in the absence of restraint over the external senses, renunciation—denoted by the term "withdrawal" (*uparama*)—belongs only to one who has conquered the senses; likewise, endurance (*titikṣā*), which consists in the capacity to bear the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, belongs only to him; and concentration (*samādhāna*), characterized by abiding with single-minded devotion in Brahman due to the absence of external distraction, belongs only to him. Furthermore, faith (*śraddhā*), which takes the form of conviction in the words of the Guru and the Vedānta being taught—that Brahman alone exists and the world is illusory—belongs only to one distinguished by such qualities.

Even within the group of six beginning with tranquility (śama), the reason for their sequential order can easily be stated. It is intended that such a preeminent person (puruṣadhaureya) desires nothing other than liberation and cannot tolerate delay therein; thus, he must possess an intense longing for liberation (tīvramumukṣā). With this in mind, [the author] first states "the eternal and the non-eternal" and so forth, and immediately thereafter, "dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter."

By stating that dispassion (*vairāgya*) follows immediately after discrimination (*viveka*), it is effectively asserted—by the maxim "for that which arises immediately after another is its effect"—that dispassion is the result of discrimination. The phrase "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*) is also to be supplied subsequently: immediately after dispassion comes the attainment of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and immediately after that comes the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). ||19||
He explains the aforementioned means of proof with the words beginning "Brahman":
"The firm conviction that Brahman is real and the world is illusory is of such a nature. (20)
Thus has this discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities been described. ||201/2||
The logical sequence is as follows: this firm conviction that Brahman is real and the world is illusory is what is designated as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. || 20 ||
Commentary:

Even when there is the certainty that Brahman is eternal and the world is non-eternal, firm dispassion (*vairāgya*) does not arise, because even non-eternal pleasure is generally desired. When it is said that the world is illusory (*mithyā*), no one desires an illusory object; for those who desire a kingdom do not long for a kingdom seen in a dream.

Therefore, for the certain arising of dispassion (*vairāgya*), he does not say "Brahman is eternal and the world is non-eternal," but rather says "Brahman is real and the world is illusory" (*jagan-mithyā*). By the qualifier *viniścayaḥ*, which means "ascertainment," it is implied that this ascertainment is not undermined by any cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*). Regarding the phrase *so'yam*: "that" refers to what was mentioned as a qualification of the discriminating person (*vivekin*) in the context of "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things"; "this" refers to what was stated at the outset as "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things. This is the meaning.

That this very [knowledge] is necessarily the cause of detachment from the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to both this world and the next is indicated here by the prefix *sam* in the word *samudāhṛta*. ||201/2||
Having defined discernment (*viveka*), he defines dispassion (*vairāgya*):
"That dispassion is the loathing [of the world] which arises through seeing, hearing, and so forth. (21)
For the objects of enjoyment, beginning with the body and ending with Brahmā, are indeed impermanent. ||211/2||
The logical sequence is as follows:

that aversion (or desire for renunciation) toward the objects of enjoyment—which range from the body up to Brahman and are perceived through sight, hearing, and so forth—as being impermanent, is indeed dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 21 ||
Commentary:

By seeing the objects of enjoyment such as the body and so forth belonging to this world; by hearing of the objects of enjoyment such as the divine body and so forth belonging to the next world; and by the word "etcetera," by inferring through reasoning what is of the same kind as that which has been seen or heard.

Disgust (*jugupsā*) toward all objects of enjoyment—from the body currently being experienced up to the body of Hiraṇyagarbha, which limits the sovereignty over the fourteen worlds for a lifespan of a hundred years according to the Brahma-measure—being impermanent and illusory, such that one thinks, "May there never be a connection with such things," and possesses an unbearable perception of them as being like the excrement of a crow; that is *vairāgya*. The neuter designation "that" (*tat*) is used because of the predominance of the quality of knowledge (*vidyā*), just as in the statement, "For coolness is the very nature of water. [As it is said:
"The man who would not be repelled by the foul odor of his own body..."
What other cause for detachment could be taught to him?
Alas, what a tragedy! We are unable to speak, being constantly driven by bulls, horses, donkeys, elephants, and buffaloes, emaciated by hunger and utterly exhausted.

"Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"; "Other than the Infinite, everything is afflicted"; "When their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world"; "All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return"—these [passages] from the seventeenth chapter of the *Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa* in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, along with the summary of the essence of all Vedānta conclusions beginning with "In the womb, amidst the feces and urine of his mother," describe how those who have performed meritorious deeds, when their merit is exhausted, are cast down by those in the sky and their limbs are rendered weak.
Reflecting upon those who have fallen from heaven in the form of constellations, who indeed would not turn away from worldly desires?

The verses beginning with "yatrāsti loke gatitāratamyam" (wherein there is a gradation of states in the world) are to be reflected upon regarding the subject of detachment (*vairāgya*). The sense is that for one who contemplates—by means of examples such as the deer and others—the susceptibility of the human body and so forth to afflictions like disease, the extreme dependence of animals and the like characterized by muteness and so forth, the oppression of gods by *rākṣasas* and other beings, and the capacity of objects such as sound to bestow manifold misfortunes, a sense of revulsion toward everything that is not the Self becomes easily attained.

And this will be clarified by the author himself later on in the passage beginning with, "by the five alone, such as sound and the rest. Although the eternity of the fruit of ritual action (*karma-phala*) appears to be suggested by the observation of such scriptural texts as, "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," and "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible," there is no fault [in our position]. For, in accordance with the principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent" (*yatkṛtakaṃ tadanityam*), and following scriptural passages such as "as here [the world] built up by action," it must necessarily be admitted that the words "immortal" (*amṛta*) and "inexhaustible" (*akṣayya*) possess a restricted meaning. As it has been said:
"For the state consisting of the perfection of all beings is indeed declared to be immortality. ||211/2||
He describes the nature of tranquility (*śama*) with the words "having become dispassionate":
"Having repeatedly become dispassionate toward the multitude of sense objects by perceiving their defects... (22).
The mind’s state of being restricted to its own specific object is called tranquility (śama). ||221/2||
The repeated detachment from the multitude of sense objects through the perception of their defects, and the mind’s steady abiding upon its own objective—that is called tranquility (śama). || 22 ||
Commentary:

For a person who repeatedly perceives the defects of sense objects—such as their having a beginning and an end, being accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, and being unpleasant in their ultimate transformation—dispassion toward them becomes inevitable. Thus, the perception of the defects of sense objects is the cause of dispassion. And when that dispassion exists, the mind, remaining fixed upon its own object—whether it be with attributes (*saguṇa*) or without attributes (*nirguṇa*)—becomes steady and free from modification. By the words "having become dispassionate" (*virajya*), [the author] states that tranquility (*śama*), which consists in the state of the mind's fixedness, is produced by dispassion.
In that context, because the suffix *lyap* conveys posteriority in time, it is thereby indicated that [the action] is produced by dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 221/2 ||
He defines restraint (*dama*) as "from the objects"—that is, turning away from the objects and establishing [the senses] within their respective sockets. (23)
The restraint of both these sets of faculties is proclaimed as self-control. ||23 1/2||
The withdrawal of both types of sense organs from their objects and their stabilization within their respective sockets—that is proclaimed as *dama* (self-restraint). || 23 ||
Commentary:

It has been stated that because the mind possesses the capacity to investigate objects, it becomes detached by its own nature. However, since the external sense organs—the instruments of cognition such as the ears and others, as well as the instruments of action such as the voice and others—lack inherent capacity for that [detachment], the mind, acting as the reins, must turn back and divert the external senses—which are like horses—from the uneven paths of objects such as sound and the like, and cause them to face away from them. This consists of establishing them in their respective physical sockets, such as the ear-cavity, the nose, and the mouth, thereby bringing about their state of cessation from activity.
That which has been proclaimed as self-control (dama) consists of the restraining and so forth of the mind and the other faculties; this is stated in the Kaṭhopaniṣad:
"Know the Self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot.
Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins."
The senses are said to be the horses, and their objects are the paths; this is the meaning. (23½)
He describes cessation (*uparati*), which is to be accomplished by the restraint of the *damaru* and the external senses, with the words "external" (*bāhya*) and so forth:
"This cessation of mental activity (*vṛtti*) from not taking external objects as its support is the highest. (24)
The non-apprehension of external objects by the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) is the highest form of cessation (*uparati*). || 24 ||
Commentary:

Just as the water of a pond, having emerged through the opening of a breach in the dam, undergoes transformation into the form of fields and so forth, even so, the internal mind, having come out through the openings of the ears and other senses, gives rise to a mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of transformation into the forms of objects such as sound. The sense is that when the external senses are restrained, the internal mind does not transform into an external form. ||24||

When the mind does not take external objects as its support, then, because the duality of cold, heat, and so forth is no longer perceived, even if such states arise through the power of karma, time, and other factors, the endurance that consists in bearing them is established. Thus he says, "endurance" (sahanam):
"Endurance of all sufferings without seeking remedy, free from anxiety and lamentation—that is declared to be titikṣā. (25)
The endurance of all sufferings, preceded by a lack of remedy and free from anxiety and lamentation—that is declared to be *titikṣā*. || 25 ||

Commentary: The remedy for sufferings such as cold and heat by means of blankets, fans, and so forth, is well-established in the world. When such means are absent, there arises the thought, "What is to be done by us wretched ones? and lamentation. [The text] excludes such a state from being a means of inquiry; endurance (*titikṣā*) is that forbearance which is devoid of remedy and free from anxious thought and lamentation. This refers to the endurance of sufferings—that is, of cold, heat, and other causes of suffering.
The sense is that for a mind accompanied by anxious thought, lamentation, and the like, the capacity for inquiry is far removed. ||25||
Now, he defines *śraddhā* (faith) as the uncommon cause for the apprehension of reality, [stating] "of the scripture":
The firm conviction through the intellect that the scripture—that is, the word of the Guru—is true; that is called *śraddhā* by the wise, by means of which reality is apprehended. (26)
The ascertainment of truth regarding the scripture and the words of the teacher is called *śraddhā* by the virtuous; it is by means of this that the reality is perceived. || 26 ||
Commentary:

Even in the world, if there is a lack of trust in the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), a person will not act in accordance with them, whether in deliberation or other matters; how much more so in the case of the subject matter of the scriptures, which transcends the senses? Therefore, that [faith] is the supreme cause. For it is said in the *Gītā*:
"O scorcher of foes, those men who have no faith in this dharma..."
"Without reaching Me, they return to the path of the cycle of death.

Thus, one who is tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, and patient, being instructed by the Guru and the Vedāntas that Brahman alone is the single reality, that alone is You, and everything else is false, places faith in this very truth, thinking, "This is exactly so. No other person lacking such means can do so; therefore, faith is subsequently enumerated as having the words of the Guru and the Vedāntas as its object. [The] Śāstra...

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) which understands that the scripture beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the words of the Guru, and the statements following them—such as "You are not a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*), but rather the Supreme Brahman whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated; everything else is false"—are true and convey an uncontradicted meaning, there arises a firm conviction (*avadhāraṇā*). That by which a reality is perceived is called "faith" (*śraddhā*) by the wise. ||26||

Only for one possessing such faith does meditative absorption (samādhāna) become perfectly accomplished; therefore, he describes that absorption immediately thereafter with the word "perfectly" (samyak):
"The constant, perfect establishment of the intellect within the pure Brahman is called 'absorption' (samādhāna), and not the pampering of the mind. (27)
The continuous, perfect stabilization of the intellect upon the pure Brahman at all times is called "concentration" (samādhi); it is certainly not the pampering of the mind. || 27 ||
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states:

Although no distinction is perceived in such a state of composure with respect to the constant condition of one's own object (*svalakṣya*), nevertheless, by means of this [instruction]—"having repeatedly become dispassionate toward sense-objects through the perception of their defects, [one attains] a constant condition in one's own object"—it is shown that from whatever cause the mind wanders, being fickle and unsteady:
"From whatever cause the mind wanders, being fickle and unsteady," [and so forth].
Restraining it from here and there, one should bring it under control within the self alone.
Thus, according to the teaching of the *Gītā*, a specific effort is required during the state of tranquility (*śama*) for the stabilization of the mind, which consists of volition and doubt.

For this very reason, the phrase "the constant and perfect establishment of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is determination (*adhyavasāya*), in the pure Brahman" indicates here that the internal organ is to be freed from volition and doubt. It is precisely for this reason that the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) is set aside and the word "intellect" (*buddhi*), characterized by the function of ascertainment, is employed. Furthermore, by the expression "in the pure Brahman," that which is devoid of all attributes (*nirguṇa*) and liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is intended.

At the occasion of defining *śama*, by the phrase "remaining in a fixed state within its own object," it is possible to speak of the tranquility (*śāntatva*) of the mind even when it abides in a fixed state while possessing qualities (*saguṇa*). *Śama* is said to be the means (*sādhana*), whereas *samādhāna* (concentration) is its fruit—that is, its full maturation.

Just as in the world people pacify children who are crying excessively by giving them what they desire, so too, allowing the mind to wander at will along the path of sense objects is not concentration; thus he says, "but not the pampering of the mind" (*na tu cittasya lālanam*). Alternatively—
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths, must be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort. (1)
O best among the powerful, by means of the strength of one's own human effort, one should cause the mind that has entered into unwholesome states to descend into wholesome ones alone. (2)
The mind of a living being, like that of a child, moves from the unwholesome to the wholesome, and from that as well to the other; therefore, one should move it by force.
One should quickly soothe the child-like mind with the consolation of equanimity—not abruptly, but gradually—through the effort of human exertion. (4)
Thus, according to the method of the *Vasiṣṭha*, either the shaking or the fondling [of the mind] is required beforehand as a means for attaining tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities.

However, this is not the case during the state of the resulting absorption (*samādhi*); for at that time, even without further practice, it is sufficient—by the very effort exerted during the period of cultivating tranquility and the rest—for the mind, whose external tendencies have been attenuated, to be established in the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) state by merely withdrawing it from the qualified (*saguṇa*) state. ||27||

Only for one adorned with such a collection of means does the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutva) arise, and not for anyone else; thus, he now describes the state of seeking liberation: "The desire to be released from the bonds beginning with egoity and ending with the body—which are imagined by ignorance—through the realization of one's own true nature, is the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutā). (28)

The desire to be liberated from the bonds beginning with egoism and ending with the body—all of which are imagined through ignorance—by means of the realization of one's own true nature, is *mumukṣutā* (the state of desiring liberation). 28.
Commentary:
Among these— the eyes and other senses— within the body,
the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) abides through the conceit "I am," by means of its luminous radiance.

By the statement "that is to be known as *ahaṅkāra*," the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) endowed with the reflection of consciousness is *ahaṅkāra*. Alternatively, the experiencer, the individual soul (*jīva*), is *ahaṅkāra*, which is named the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*). In the definition of one's own self—wherein one identifies through the slight fragments of happiness experienced during sleep, thinking "I am happy"—how could that which is named the sheath of bliss be the Self?

Because it has been so stated, it is possible to say that even for that [mind], its being imagined by ignorance (*ajñāna-kalpitatva*) and its being a modification (*vikāratva*) due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the mind are secondary (*gauṇa*). And thus, in order to liberate from—meaning to abandon and sublate—the bonds beginning with the sheath of bliss (*ānanda-kośa*) and ending with the sheaths of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), and food (*annamaya*), which one regards as the self prior to the direct realization of one's true nature; and so that, through the awakening to one's own true nature, the sense of "I" (*ahantā*) may no longer exist there—that desire is *mumukṣutā* (the state of desiring liberation). For, in the awakening to one's own true nature...

The meaning is that, according to the Śruti text, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?", there is an absolute cessation of bondage consisting of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), due to the non-appearance of anything whatsoever distinct from oneself. ||28||

This desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) is threefold: weak, middling, and intense. Even though liberation consists of eternal bliss, the very desire for liberation is difficult to attain for those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are permeated by worldly latent impressions (vāsanā). That [desire] which arises at the time of hearing the scriptures on the supreme self (adhyātma-śāstra) does not produce its effect.

When a person, having perceived the defects in worldly objects through the discrimination born immediately after hearing [the teachings], attains detachment toward them, renounces all actions according to the rules, and proceeds to approach a teacher for the sake of inquiry—at that time, the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) that arose during the hearing of the spiritual scriptures is merely temporary; being weak, it is indeed worthy of the name "weak," yet it attains the state of being "middling."

To the extent that one’s dispassion becomes intense, the mind becomes tranquil, and one desires to attain meditative absorption (samādhi), and when the Guru is pleased with this, thinking, "May this person quickly cross the ocean of worldly existence," then that person—having become one whose desire for liberation has increased and who, being the primary candidate (adhikārī), desires nothing other than liberation characterized by eternal bliss and cannot endure any delay therein—quickly attains the fruit. Thus he says, beginning with "Manda": "Even if it is of a mild or middling form, through dispassion, tranquility (śama), and so forth, and through the grace of the Guru, this [desire] increases and gives birth to the fruit. (29)

The sequence is as follows: even when of a dull or middling form, she (the intellect) produces fruit; this very [intellect], having increased through the grace of the Guru, through dispassion, and through tranquility and the like, [produces the highest fruit]. 29.
Commentary:

And thus, although the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) consists of the wish for *mokṣa*, it is only when that [wish] has increased that it produces the fruit; by this it is stated that a person must exert effort for the sake of its increase, for the sake of detachment from sense-objects, the six qualities such as tranquility (*śama*), and the attainment of the Guru’s grace. ||29||

Among the fourfold means [to liberation], he says that everything exists only when the second and the fourth are present, and not otherwise: "Dispassion"—that is to say: "In one who possesses both dispassion and an intense desire for liberation, it is only in such a person that tranquility and the other [means] become meaningful and bear fruit. (30)
The sequence beginning with tranquility (śama) would be meaningful and fruitful only for one who possesses intense dispassion and the desire for liberation. || 30 ||
Commentary:

Regarding the statement "tranquility and the others possess their respective meanings," the phrase "tranquility and the others" means the words "tranquility and the others. The sense is that the conventional usage—that such a person possesses tranquility and the others—is meaningful. This refers to one who bears the designations "peaceful," "self-controlled," and so forth; that is, one who possesses intense dispassion (*tīvra-vairāgya*) and intense yearning for liberation (*tīvra-mumukṣutā*), because it is precisely this intense yearning for liberation that constitutes the fruit of tranquility and the other qualities.

If there is an intense desire for liberation (tīvramumukṣutva), then, since the fruit cannot be obtained without the means, the cause is inferred from the effect; thus, it is easy to say that he possesses tranquility (śama) and the other qualities. In this way, when intense dispassion (tīvra-vairāgya)—the means consisting of tranquility and so forth—is known to exist in him, then because the fruit necessarily follows when the means are present, his possession of tranquility and the rest becomes unavoidable.

And thus, when there is the accomplishment of tranquility (*śama*) and the other means, and when there is the state of intense desire for liberation (*tīvramumukṣutva*)—which is the fruit of intense dispassion (*tīvravairāgya*) and the other qualities—the meaning is that [this desire for liberation] itself stands unassailable, situated between its own means and its fruit. The distinction is this: when there is intense dispassion, the terms "tranquility" and so forth are meaningful; when there is intense desire for liberation, "tranquility" and the others possess their fruit. Since tranquility and the rest, which reside in another part of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are difficult to discern, it was stated that they are to be understood through their cause and their effect.

When it is asked how it is to be known that a person has himself accomplished peace and so forth, the sense is that it is known when the abundant cause—intense dispassion—and the distinguished result—intense yearning for liberation—are present; thus, both the cause and the effect are indicators in oneself and in others.

Intense dispassion toward objects of enjoyment is held to be that perception which regards them as unbearable, like the excrement of a crow. The wise say that the very perception of defects in objects of enjoyment is the repository of the intensity of dispassion.

Thus, the intensity of dispassion and its means have been described in this compendium of the essence of the conclusions of all Vedānta. Intensity in the desire for liberation is simply its full development; that has already been explained [previously]. (30)
Where there is dullness regarding these two—dispassion and the desire for liberation—there, tranquility and the rest exist as mere appearances, like water in a desert. (31)
The logical connection is as follows:
where there is a dullness of both these qualities—dispassion and the desire for liberation—there, tranquility and the like exist merely as appearances, like water in a desert. || 31 ||
Commentary:

When there is a dullness or merely temporary nature regarding these two—dispassion and the desire for liberation—in a person, it is like water in a desert. Just as during the summer season, when the fierce rays of the sun strike the desert land, one who is at a distance may have the illusion that "there is water there," yet there is no attainment of water and consequently no cessation of thirst; on the contrary, for the weary traveler, going toward that water with the thought that it exists only increases his exhaustion—even so it is when intense dispassion and the desire for liberation are absent.

The intention is that in that state, tranquility (*śama*) and so forth exist as mere appearances; they are not the actual fruit of tranquility, nor is he designated by other terms such as "the peaceful one" (*śānta*) and so on. ||31||

Thus, having described the qualifications—discrimination and so forth—for one qualified for the inquiry into Brahman, which consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and functions to determine the purport of all the Vedāntas upon the non-dual Brahman, who is identical with the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, he states that devotion (*bhakti*), which is the direct means to the direct realization of the Self and is achievable through the aforementioned inquiry:
"Among the collection of causes for liberation, devotion alone is the most important.
Devotion is defined as the contemplation of one's own true nature. (32)

The logical sequence is as follows: among the collection of causes for liberation, devotion alone is the most weighty; therefore, the contemplation of one's own true nature is itself designated as "devotion. || 32 ||
Commentary:

"Contemplation" (nididhyāsana) is said to be the inquiry into one's own true nature (svasvarūpānusandhāna), because it is the direct means for the immediate realization (sākṣātkāra) of that very [nature]. The meaning heard through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—that "That is the Self, Thou art That" (sa ātmā tattvamasi)—is that Brahman, which is your own nature, is indeed you. The inquiry into that, which consists of a continuous flow of similar mental impressions (sajātīya-pratyaya-pravāha) unobstructed by dissimilar impressions (vijātīya-pratyaya) and which maintains the state of such contemplation (bhāvanā), is the uncommon cause for immediate realization; this is the intended sense.

The meaning is that while tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] are causes for knowledge by way of inquiry (*vicāra*) and by way of meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*), this [devotion] is so directly. For this very reason, it has been stated that among the causal complex—that is, within the collection of means for that knowledge which is the manifestor of liberation—devotion alone is the most important, because it is the direct cause. And that causal complex consists of everything from discrimination (*viveka*) up to meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*). [32]
He states the opinion of others:
"Others have declared that devotion is the contemplation of the reality of one's own self. (321/2)
Others have declared that devotion consists in the inquiry into the true nature of one's own self. (321)

Commentary: "Svātman" refers to one's own self, that is, the individual soul (*jīva*). "Tattva" is the state of being that [Self], meaning the state of being the referent of the word "That" (*tatpadavācyārthatva*), which is to say, the state of being the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*). "Anusandhāna" of that is the meditation upon it as non-different, even though an actual difference exists; this is what is meant by "meditation with the sense of identity" (*ahaṅgrahopāsana*). Others have declared that this is "devotion" (*bhakti*); however, this indicates that this form—which is preceded by the notion of difference and is of the nature of delusion—does not possess the status of primary devotion. (321/2)

He states the duty for one who has been endowed with the previously mentioned means: "Endowed with the aforementioned means and desiring to know the reality, he should approach a wise Guru from whom comes liberation from bondage. (331/2)

The logical connection is as follows: one who is endowed with the aforementioned means, desiring to know the reality of the self, should approach a wise teacher from whom liberation from bondage is obtained. || 33 ||

Commentary: "Endowed with the aforementioned means"—the word "person" (*pumān*) is to be supplied as the subject. This refers to one who is endowed with, or possessed of, those means such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest, which have been described as the instruments for inquiry. Desiring to know the reality (*tattva*) of the Self—that is, desiring knowledge of one's own true nature—one should approach, or go for refuge to, a teacher (*guru*). Who is he? A teacher who provides instruction. Of what kind? "Wise" (*prājña*): *prajñā* is preeminent, unsurpassed knowledge or realization, namely the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman;
it is the realization of the identity between Brahman and the Self once both have been purified.

Since it will be stated later that "the modification which is non-conceptual and pure consciousness is called *prajñā*," one who possesses this is *prajña*; he himself is the *prājña*. The meaning is: "him who is established in Brahman. By this, he states the fruit for himself: from whatever kind of guru [one receives] the liberation from bondage—the specific relinquishing of bondage, which is imagined through ignorance and extends from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) to the body—so, by approaching such a guru, liberation in the form of the cessation of bondage is accomplished through the knowledge of one's own true nature (*yāthātmya-jñāna*) born from his instruction; this is the sense. ||331/2||
He characterizes such a Guru with the words beginning "one learned in the Vedas" (śrotriya):
"One learned in the Vedas, free from vice, undisturbed by desire, who is the highest among the knowers of Brahman;
who has ceased [from worldly activity] in Brahman, is tranquil, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. (341/2)

The sequence is as follows: he who is learned in the Vedas, free from crookedness, unassailed by desire, the best among the knowers of Brahman, withdrawn into Brahman, peaceful, like a fire without fuel. ||34||
Commentary:

According to the rule taught by Pāṇini, "śrotriyaśchando'dhīte" (one who has studied the Veda is called *śrotriya*), the meaning is "one who has studied the Upaniṣads. This is because only one who, having studied the Upaniṣads, has performed inquiry into their meaning possesses the cause for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). "Avṛjinaḥ" means "sinless. [As stated:
"Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed..."
Nor can one whose mind is not tranquil attain this even through wisdom.

Thus says the Śruti. Regarding this, he states the reason: "one who is not struck by desire" (*akāmahata*). One who is "struck by desire" (*kāmahata*) is one who is afflicted by the longing for sense-objects; the meaning is that his true nature is obscured. One who is not so struck is "not struck by desire. He who does not know the bliss of his own nature might, at times, even commit sin in order to attain that external pleasure. However, for this most excellent knower of Brahman, because the bliss of his own nature is being directly realized, sense-objects turn away from him—just as objects turn away from a person who abstains from food, yet the craving for taste remains; but that craving ceases upon seeing the Supreme.

Thus, according to the teaching of the *Gītā*, the state of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahatatva*), which consists in the cessation of passion, is indeed established; therefore, freedom from sin resides in him, since desire alone is the cause of sin. As it is said in the *Gītā*: "Then, O Vārṣṇeya, by what impelled does this man commit sin, even against his will, as if constrained by force?"

Thus questioned by Arjuna, the Blessed One said: "This desire, this anger, born of the quality of *rajas*—know this to be the great devourer, the great sinner, the enemy here. And so forth. "Stilled in Brahman" means one whose mind has dissolved into Brahman; therefore, he is peaceful like a fire without fuel. Just as a fire becomes peaceful and devoid of flames in the absence of fuel, so too is he peaceful because his mental modifications (*vṛtti*) do not rest upon external objects, and he is peaceful because his consciousness is firmly established in the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman; the meaning is that he is free from all transformation.

In this context, the qualifying attributes such as being a śrotriya do not function as differentiators, because in one who is the most excellent knower of Brahman, the states of being a non-śrotriya, being sinful, and being overcome by desire are impossible. Rather, since they can exist as actualities, they serve to indicate such a Guru; thus, they should be understood as constituting a definition of essential nature (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa). ||34 1/2||
He is the ocean of causeless compassion and the kinsman of the virtuous who bow before him. ||35||
The lineage [is as follows]: he who is an ocean of causeless compassion, a kinsman to the virtuous and to those who bow before him. ||35||

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): That which has no cause is "causeless" (*ahetukī*). Such compassion (*dayā*)—meaning the desire to eliminate the suffering of others—is its "ocean," that is, its locus. In the case of another compassionate person, compassion arises toward others upon seeing their suffering because one has oneself also experienced suffering; therefore, the term "causeless" is used to exclude that. However, for this [Buddha], due to the power of his knowledge, there is no occurrence of suffering either from himself or from others. Thus, the sense is that at the time of his emergence from meditative equipoise, his sole intention is: "May people cross the ocean of cyclic existence."

"Bandhu" means one who removes suffering. For whom? For "those who bow"—that is, for virtuous persons who have become humble. By this, it is indicated that they teach only after fully ascertaining the characteristics of the disciple. Indeed, it is heard there [in the scriptures]: "This should not be given to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to a rogue; it is not to be given to one who is not a disciple," and so forth. And it is recorded in the Gītā: "This must never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who reviles Me."
This is the approach to the Guru:
having propitiated that Guru with devotion, bowing low with services of humility, and having obtained his favor, one should ask him about that which is to be known by oneself. (36)

The lineage [of teachers]: Having propitiated that Guru with devotion through humble service and modesty, and having obtained the favor of that Guru, one should inquire about what is to be known regarding the Self. || 36 ||

Commentary: Devotion (*bhakti*) is affection for those worthy of worship; it is a mental quality. One who is "inclined" (*prahva*) by that [devotion] is one whose body is bent, characterized by gestures that manifest it, with palms joined in reverence (*baddhāñjalipuṭa*). "By means of humility and service" (*praśrayasevanaiḥ*): the meaning is "by means of both humility (*praśraya*) and services (*sevanāni*)."

In that regard, "humility" (*praśraya*) consists of modest speech; "service" (*sevanāni*) includes prostrating with eight limbs, massaging his feet, carrying out his instructions, and so forth. Having propitiated and served him with such service, and having gained his favor through that upright devotion so that he is turned toward him, one should remain in his presence according to the rules and as directed at the appropriate time, and then ask about that which is to be known by oneself—the object of one's desire to know regarding the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*).

By the phrase "having propitiated [him] with devotion, humility, and services," the purity of the three instruments (trikaraṇa-śuddhi)—consisting of purity in thought, speech, and body—of the one who propitiates is stated. ||36||

Out of compassion, the Blessed One shows the manner of worship through verbal prayer preceded by devotion to those who desire to know, from the words "O Lord, salutations to You" up to "speaking thus":
"O Lord, salutations to You, O kinsman of those who bow; O ocean of compassion, [I am] fallen into the ocean of worldly existence."
Lift me up with your own sidelong glance,
which is straight and showered with the nectar of supreme compassion.

The sequence [of the verse]: O Lord, salutations to You, the kinsman of those who bow; O ocean of compassion, lift me up—who have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence—with Your straight glance of a personal side-long look, which rains down the nectar of supreme mercy. 37.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): *natalokabandho*—O friend of the world that bows, O kinsman of people who have performed prostrations, O deliverer from suffering; [this is] the vocative address to Him. *Svāmin*, *prabho* (Lord, Master), *te* (to You), *namaḥ* (salutation); the remainder [of the sentence] is "let there be an act of bowing. Since You are the deliverer from the suffering of the world that bows, the sense is: "Therefore, I bow to You for the sake of liberation from suffering. He states the reason for this by means of the address *kāruṇyasindho* (O ocean of compassion). This has been explained in the passage beginning with *ahetukadayāsindhuḥ* (the ocean of causeless mercy).

He reports his own suffering, stating that he has fallen into the ocean of existence (*bhavābdhi*); the meaning is that he has fallen into the sea of *saṃsāra*, which is crowded with the calamities of birth, old age, and death. Now he prays for its cessation, saying, "Lift me up" (*mām uddhara*); the meaning is: "Make me free from the bondage of birth and so forth. Therein, he requests the means: "By Your glance" (*ātmīyakaṭākṣadṛṣṭyā*); the meaning is: "by the corner of Your own eye. The underlying thought is: "When You, whose every impurity has been shaken off by the direct realization of Brahman, cast Your purifying glance upon me, I shall be liberated from all sins and cross over the ocean of *saṃsāra*."
For it has been said:
"Those whose intellect, culminating in direct experience, proceeds toward reality—
all those who come within the range of such vision are liberated from all sins."

By this, the manner of discipline is shown: that a disciple must not stand directly in front of the Guru. Furthermore, a full gaze is merely a side-long glance (kaṭākṣapāta); thus, there is also the sense that "I desire that [glance]. The meaning is: "May I become entirely purified and liberated from suffering when the mind, which is immersed in the bliss of the eternally pure Brahman, falls fully upon me through the medium of the corners of [the Guru's] eyes."

Alternatively, "with her own side-glance" means by her glance of personal favor. By the adjective "straight" (*ṛjvyā*), meaning naturally simple, the following intention is suggested: just as in the world one who has fallen into deep water is pulled out by grasping a straight rope or staff, so too do I, by grasping your long, long glance, emerge from the ocean of *saṃsāra*. This is the implied sense.

Just as rays emerge from the solar disc or a lamp, gathering together like a rope, so too do the rays issue forth from the eye because it is composed of light (*tejas*). The sense is that when these rays reach [the person], they uplift him because his mind is united with one who is established in Brahman. Through the rain of the nectar of supreme compassion—*atikāruṇya* meaning extreme compassion, which is itself likened to "nectar" (*sudhā*) because it removes all suffering—the [person is uplifted].

"Sudhā" means nectar; that vision in which there is a shower [of it] on all sides is "the shower of the nectar of extreme compassion. By that shower of the nectar of extreme compassion—the fact being well known that by the raining down of nectar a person becomes exempt from old age, death, and so forth, as it is famous in the *Rāmāyaṇa* that the monkeys who died in battle were restored to life by the shower of nectar caused by Indra—such a shower of the nectar of compassion from one established in Brahman will grant the state of being exempt from uncontracted old age, death, and so forth. This is the intended meaning. ||37||
Unable to endure any delay in his own liberation, he manifests his own intense yearning for emancipation, which is difficult to restrain:
"Scorched by the forest fire of the irresistible cycle of existence and tossed about by the winds of adverse karma..."
Protect me, who am terrified and have come to you for refuge; I know no other protector from death.
The logical connection is as follows:

since I know no other refuge, therefore, protect me—who am scorched by the forest fire of this irresistible saṃsāra, tossed about by the winds of misfortune, and terrified of death—having come to you for shelter. || 38 ||

Commentary: Saṃsāra itself is a forest fire (*vanānala*) because, like a forest fire, it pervades everything and is the cause of suffering. It is "difficult to ward off" (*durvāra*), meaning it cannot be prevented without the knowledge produced by your excellent instruction; that is, it is impossible to stop on one's own. Furthermore, it is a "difficult-to-ward-off" forest fire of saṃsāra, and by it [we] are tormented—that is, burnt. It is well known that when a forest fire is accompanied by wind, its capacity to pervade extensively and cause heat is established.

Likewise, "by the winds of misfortune" means by those very misfortunes—the sins—which act as adverse winds; being "shaken," or repeatedly agitated, by them. If the wind were favorable, it might carry him elsewhere, but since the wind is adverse, it either casts him into fire or casts the fire upon him. With the intention that for one scorched by a forest fire, there may be liberation from suffering through a shower of nectar, the epithet "having rained down the nectar of supreme compassion upon sight" was previously given.

In this context, without forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound, one may also say: "by means of the glance" (*dṛṣṭyā*) as the instrument, and "by the showering of the nectar of great compassion" (*atikāruṇyasudhābhivṛṣṭyā*), that is, by the raining down of nectar. Thus, the syntactical connection is: "Protect me, who am scorched by the forest fire of death. And in this way, the prior connection is: "Lift me up with your own straight side-long glance. Furthermore, the subsequent connection is: "By that [glance], through the showering of the nectar of great compassion, protect me, who am scorched by the forest fire of *saṃsāra*, from death."

The construction applies to both parts: "Protect me, who am afraid of death, who have approached you, and who have come for refuge from death. The sense is that, through your grace, once self-knowledge has arisen, my death in the form of the departure of the vital breaths from the body is no longer possible; for the Śruti says: "His vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here."

And thus, because it has been said, "Birth is certain for one who has died," and since the absence of birth is established upon the absence of death, the underlying meaning is: "By your grace, may I be liberated from *saṃsāra*, which consists of the continuous flow of birth and death. He reveals his own lack of any other refuge in order to draw the Guru's attention: "Because I know no other protector" (*śaraṇyam anyaṃ yad ahaṃ na jāne*). Since I know no protector other than you, the sense is: "This person has no other refuge; therefore, you should not remain indifferent toward him. ||38||
With two verses, he says that for those like you, compassion toward us is indeed sincere:
"The great ones dwell in peace;
the virtuous live like the spring season, acting for the welfare of the world."
Having themselves crossed the formidable ocean of existence, they cause other people as well to cross it without any motive. ||39||
This is the very nature of the great-souled, by its own accord, to be inclined toward dispelling the fatigue of others;
for this moon itself protects the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun. (40)

The great holy ones dwell in peace like springtime, practicing for the welfare of the world; having themselves crossed the formidable ocean of existence, they ferry other people across as well, without any selfish motive. (39)

This is the very nature of the great-souled: that they are spontaneously inclined toward dispelling the labors of others; just as this moon indeed protects by itself the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun. 40.

Commentary: In the rainy season there is the affliction of rain; in summer, heat; at the beginning of autumn, there is comfort, because the two months ending with Kārttika and beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa are proclaimed to be the "fangs of Yama"; in the cold and dewy seasons, there is cold; and the spring season, a source of fragrant flowers, produces happiness for the world in its entirety. Thus it is said to be "like spring," because at that time there is an absence of rain, heat, cold, disease, and so forth.

Just as that season produces only happiness, so too those who extend happiness to the world—being peaceful, with minds free from modification, and for that very reason great; possessing the direct realization of the unlimited Brahman, and consequently being "existent" (sat) through non-difference from such true Brahman according to the Vedic scripture, "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—have crossed over that ocean of worldly existence (bhavārṇava), which is itself formidable and terrifying; the meaning is that they are no longer subject to transmigratory existence.
