Because they have attained all their desires, they lack any personal motive; thus, "without cause" means without a motive. The sense is that they rescue others as well—those submerged in the ocean of existence. How can they rescue them without a cause? For in the case of an inherent nature (*svabhāva*), no external cause need be sought.

The intention is that it is not appropriate to ask what the cause of sweetness is in sugar, because it is inherent to it. "Devoted to dispelling the toil of others" means: the toil of others is their suffering; its "dispelling" is its removal. The term "devoted" (*pravaṇa*) refers primarily to the state of being; thus, "the state of being devoted" (*pravaṇabhāva*), "devotion" (*pravaṇatā*), or "attachment" (*saktatā*)—that is, the sense of being intent upon it—is the very nature of the great-souled ones, occurring spontaneously.

The meaning is that in this matter, such things as the instigation of others are not required. He provides an illustration for this with the words "the moon" and so forth: the moon—the one well-known to have rays of nectar—is situated nearby; though not prompted by another, he himself protects the earth, which has been scorched on all sides by the harsh, intense radiance of the sun (arka). The word "kila" indicates what is commonly known. ||40||

Thus, with a humble appearance, speech conforming to that, and devotion manifested thereby, the distressed one—having no other refuge—desires with fortitude to request the supreme teacher, who purifies him by raining down the nectar of grace and compassion through his glances, to instruct him in the liberation from his own bondage. He does so with the words beginning "O Brahmānanda":

"Sprinkle me with the nectars of your words, which are pleasant to the ear, pure, cool, and white, released from the jar of your speech, and permeated by the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss."
O Lord, this man is scorched by the flames of the forest fire of Your misfortune;
blessed are those who have been made worthy recipients and accepted at the very moment they came within the range of Your glance. 41.

O Lord, sprinkle this [servant]—who is scorched by the flames of the forest-fire of worldly suffering—with the nectar-like words that are pleasing to the ear, pure, cool, white, and released from the jar of Your speech, which are permeated by the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss; those who have been made worthy recipients and accepted by You at the very moment of Your glance are truly blessed. 41.
Commentary:

O Lord, O All-Powerful One! Those persons who have become vessels—that is, the recipients—of the momentary arrival of Your glance, meaning the arrival of that compassionate look; or alternatively, those who have become the locus, the support, for the momentary contact of Your glance—that is, Your eye—for even a mere instant, being the targets falling within the range of Your eyes; they alone are blessed and have achieved their life's purpose, having been accepted as Your own.
Therefore, I too, having been struck by Your glance, am most blessed and most fallen; desiring to cool the heat of the fires of worldly existence very quickly, I pray thus—so he indicates.

By the maxim, "Who can ever be satiated with that which is most excellent," You have accepted me as the object of Your side-glance. "Bhavatāpa" means the heat of worldly existence; it is the sorrow of *saṃsāra* itself, which is like a forest fire (*dāvadahana*). I am scorched—that is, utterly consumed—by its flames. This person standing before me is [to be made] a "rasa," meaning one who tastes the nectar that is the bliss of Brahman itself. Therefore, by means of those [glances] which are permeated by the experience of That and are thus purified by virtue of removing all impurities, [may I be so transformed].

They are *pavitraiḥ* (purifying), according to the Smṛti: "Indeed, nothing purifying like knowledge is found here. Like such knowledge, these sentences are pure because they consist of the instruction of that knowledge which removes all sins. They are *suśītaiḥ* (very cool) because they destroy internal torments—namely, those pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), the divine (*ādhidevika*), and the elemental (*ādhibhautika*). They are *sitaiḥ* (white) because they are stainless, leading exclusively to the path of *sattva* by means of turning one away from the paths of *rajas* and *tamas*.

"By those poured from the jar of your speech"—your speech is *yuṣmadvāk*; that faculty of speech, its locus, or the mouth itself is the jar (*kalaśa*), and from it flow the nectars of words. Thus, "by those poured" means by those emitted or released; "pleasing to the ear" means bringing joy to the ears; "by the nectars of words" means by the words themselves which are nectars. "Sprinkle me" means "sprinkle"; the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used here for the sake of the root meaning itself.

Purity, extreme coolness, whiteness, and being released from the jar are common to both [the nectar] and the sentences; thus, the sentences are metaphorically identified with nectar. The reason for their purity is that they are "imbued with the experience of the essence of Brahman-bliss" and "pleasing to the ear. By this it is meant that even at the time of hearing them, they produce bliss; what then need be said of the immediate bliss that arises when one experiences them by contemplating their meaning? ||41||
He clarifies the fear previously mentioned in the verse beginning with "fearful and having sought refuge," for the sake of accomplishing grace upon himself suddenly. He asks:
"How may I cross this ocean of existence? What is my destination? Which is the means? and so forth.
O Lord, out of compassion, do not disregard me; inflict the wound of the suffering of saṃsāra upon me. ||42||

The sequence of thought: How may I cross this ocean of existence? What is my course? What means is there? I know nothing at all; protect me out of compassion! O Lord, bring about the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. 42.

Commentary: "How shall I cross this ocean of worldly existence, which is entangled in a manifold and irresistible web of sufferings? If I continue to behave in this very manner, what will be my destination? What can I possibly attain? The sense is that it is nothing but suffering in every respect. Therefore, what means exists? What is the method for crossing this ocean of worldly existence? As for me, I know nothing at all. Protect me; guard me who am thus terrified. He clearly prays for protection when he says, 'Bring about the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra.
The meaning is: utterly uproot the sorrow of worldly existence. (42)
Now, with two verses beginning with "tathā," he instructs the teacher on what must be done:

"Having beheld his own refugee who speaks thus, tormented by the heat of the forest fire of saṃsāra, the Great-Souled One should immediately grant him fearlessness with a gaze moistened by the essence of compassion. (43)

Therefore, out of compassion alone, the wise teacher should impart the instruction on reality to one who has approached him for refuge, who seeks liberation, who acts according to what has been taught, whose mind is tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint. (44)

The Great-Souled One (the Guru), beholding with a gaze moistened by the essence of compassion his own seeker who has come for refuge—speaking thus and scorched by the heat of the forest fire of saṃsāra—should immediately grant him fearlessness. || 43 ||

That wise one should indeed compassionately impart the instruction on reality to him who has approached for service, who desires liberation, who acts according to what is taught, whose mind is tranquil, and who is endowed with peace. 44.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states:

By the expression "speaking thus," it is shown that because his internal qualification can be correctly known through the activity of speech, the teachers must first ascertain the qualified disciple before performing such acts as the granting of fearlessness and instruction.

Perceiving his own self—who had come for refuge, scorched by the heat of the forest fire of *saṃsāra*—as one who has arrived seeking protection, and gazing upon him with a vision moistened by the essence of compassion, the Great Soul, whose intellect is not small, should immediately grant fearlessness (*abhaya*). By this, it is implied that those who are terrified must be liberated from their fear at once. The underlying thought is that only when a person’s fear has ceased through the gift of fearlessness does the capacity to grasp the taught meaning and so forth become possible.

It has been said that one who is capable must not allow fear to persist for a long time in one who is afraid; thus, he spoke "at once. Having stated that the granting of safety to the frightened must first be performed, the author indicates with the words "the wise one" (*vidvān*) and so forth that instruction follows subsequently, according to one's qualification.

He is the wise one, the best among the knowers of Brahman, the teacher; to the seeker of liberation who has approached him in due form—that is, gone into his presence according to the rules—to the one who desires release, and to the virtuous one who acts as instructed—that is, who correctly performs what has been enjoined. By this, his status as a disciplined person (*śiṣṭatva*) is stated, for it has been said: "Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain Him through wisdom."

The sense is that the teacher must examine the disciple’s status as a *śrotriya* (learned in the Vedas), his integrity (*avṛjinatva*), and his freedom from desires other than the desire for liberation (*mokṣakāma*). To one whose mind is tranquil—having become detached from all objects of enjoyment from the body up to Brahman; whose mind is fixed steadily upon its own true goal; and who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*)—meaning his external senses are restrained—thereby the sixfold discipline beginning with tranquility (*śamādi-ṣaṭka*) is indicated. These are the qualifications of the candidate.

To him, who is adorned with a multitude of virtues such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the like, one should indeed impart instruction in reality (*tattvopadeśa*) out of compassion and with the desire to remove his suffering; for one whose desires are fulfilled has no other longing—thus the particle *eva* (indeed) is placed out of its syntactic order (*bhinnakrama*). The sense is that once a qualified recipient is found, one must not remain indifferent; for when the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is bestowed upon a worthy vessel, it becomes established for the sake of blessing the world.

Thus, the fruit of the instruction is the uninterrupted lineage of the knowledge of Brahman—which removes ignorance, the cause of all evils—and the liberation of one's own disciple. In this regard, the composition of the treatise in the form of a dialogue between teacher and disciple serves to facilitate the ascent of reality into the intellect of the listeners. For this very reason, indeed, the Śruti also employs narratives (ākhyāyikā) here and there.
By means of this, we are able to understand effortlessly all the characteristics of the teacher, the characteristics of the disciple, the points to be questioned, and so forth. ||44||

The supremely compassionate Guru, wishing to instantly dispel the fear shown by the disciple through such words as "How may I cross this ocean of existence?", said: "Do not fear! "Do not fear, O wise one; for you there is no calamity. There exists a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
I shall point out to you that very path by which the ascetics have gone to the further shore. (45)

The sequence of meaning: "O wise one, do not fear; there is no destruction for you. There is a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. I shall point out to you that very path by which the ascetics have gone to its further shore. (45)

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "O wise one, do not fear; let there be no fear for you"—thus, by saying this, He has suddenly granted fearlessness. By addressing him as "O wise one" (*vidvan*), He indicates that having attained discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth, one must realize that without the grace of the Guru, there is no crossing over suffering; furthermore, He suggests that since you have come to Me, you surely know what ought to be known. For one such as you, who acts rightly as prescribed, there is no downfall, according to the Smṛti: "O dear one, no one who performs auspicious deeds ever goes to a miserable state."

"Therefore, how shall I cross over, and what is my destination? Do not fear"—this is the meaning. Having thus consoled him by saying, "Do not fear; there is no calamity for you who seek your own welfare," he states the answer to the question, "What is the means? namely: "There is a means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. Therein, in order to produce right conviction, he describes that means along with its authoritative basis: "I point out—that is, I instruct—the very path by which ascetics (yatayaḥ), those striving aspirants who have renounced worldly life (saṃnyāsinaḥ), have gone to the further shore, the end of this ocean of saṃsāra. ||45||
In order to achieve intensity in the desire to hear such a path, he again indicates the means in its general form: "There exists," etc.
"There exists a certain great means that destroys the fear of saṃsāra;
by means of it, having crossed the ocean of existence, you shall attain supreme bliss. (46)
There exists a certain great means that destroys the fear of saṃsāra; by it, having crossed the ocean of existence, you shall attain supreme bliss. || 46 ||
Commentary:

There exists a certain great means for destroying the fear of saṃsāra, which is to be accomplished through many arduous practices; by that aforementioned means, having crossed the ocean of existence—the difficult-to-traverse sea of saṃsāra—and having shattered the ignorance that is its root, you will attain, or rather obtain, supreme bliss, which is infinite and eternal contentment. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that the disciple is completely satisfied with the thought: "It is indeed the cessation of suffering that you desire; however, by means of the method I am about to teach, not only will suffering be utterly ceased, but there will also be the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassed bliss for you. ||46||
He specifically points out that means: "In the Vedānta... and so forth.
Through the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta, the supreme knowledge arises;
by that, there subsequently occurs the absolute destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. (47)

The logical sequence is as follows: through the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta, supreme knowledge arises; by that, one experiences the absolute destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. || 47 ||

Commentary: The "ends of the Vedas" (*vedāntāḥ*) are the Upaniṣads. By means of an inquiry into their meaning—determined through the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya*), such as the introduction and conclusion—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is revealed; He is devoid of internal or external distinctions of a similar kind, and His nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free. Through an inquiry into Him—that is, through a mental activity conducive to His definitive determination—an "excellent knowledge" (*uttamaṃ jñānam*) arises: a definitive certainty (*nirṇaya*) that is not variegated by doubt, mental construction (*bhāvanā*), or other such defects.

By that definitive realization, there occurs the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra in its ultimate sense—a destruction of suffering that is not co-temporal with the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of any suffering that has the same locus as itself; "thereafter" means immediately following that realization, or it will come to be. ||47||
Now, he states the specific causes for such a determination, beginning with the word "faith" (śraddhā).
The speech of the Śruti directly declares that faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga are the causes of liberation for one who seeks liberation.
Or rather, for one who abides in these very [principles], there is liberation from that bondage of the body which is imagined through ignorance. 48.

The speech of the Śruti directly declares that faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga are the means for one seeking liberation to attain freedom; for one who abides in these alone, there is liberation from the bondage of the body imagined through ignorance. Or rather: [this is the meaning]. 48.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*):

Among these, *śraddhā* (faith) is defined as confidence in the Vedānta texts, the teacher, and so forth, as in the passage beginning with "confidence in the scripture and the words of the teacher. *Bhakti* (devotion) is the contemplation of one's own true nature, which is *nididhyāsana* (repeated reflection). *Dhyāna* (meditation) is aphorized as "the one-pointedness of the mental state therein" (*Yogasūtra* 3.2), and it is defined as "the constant, perfect stabilization of the purified intellect upon Brahman" (*Yogasūtra* 1.1). This is *samādhāna* (concentration).

Yoga is defined by the aphorism: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. In this regard, faith (*śraddhā*) is the cause in all cases. Among devotion (*bhakti*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and yoga, each subsequent one has the preceding one as its cause. This is because, when the fluctuations of the mind have ceased, there arises concentration (*samādhi*), and within that state, there occurs profound contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) consisting of the investigation into one's own true nature in accordance with what has been heard from scripture and the instructions of the teacher.

Alternatively, based on the verbal root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking," the term *dhyāna* refers to reflection (*manana*)—which consists of contemplation through reasoning—as the direct cause of *nididhyāsana*; or it may refer to meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*), which removes all evils that obstruct knowledge. In both these cases, the fact remains that yoga, in the form of the cessation of the mind's outward fluctuations, is indeed the cause.

Alternatively, *yoga* is that by means of which one is joined (*yujyate*) or connected with the direct realization of the Self; thus, it is devotion (*bhakti*) that is this *yoga*, or meditation (*dhyāna*) that is this *yoga*. Hence, the connection is either "the yoga of devotion" (*bhaktiyoga*) or "the yoga of meditation" (*dhyānayoga*).

For the person desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*—the sacred word of the *Śruti*—directly declares the causes of liberation, which is the cessation of bondage, in the passage: "Know [it] through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga. The meaning is that the direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) speaks thus. Alternatively, the construction may be: the *Śruti*, containing the word "know" (*avehi*), declares the direct causes—that is, the immediate reasons—for liberation, which is the knowledge that is the cause of liberation.
"Whosoever indeed, among these very things—faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga—abides, being always full of faith, possessed of devotion, a meditator, and a yogi, for him... [the result follows].

By the use of the word *adas* (that), [the author] indicates the rarity of such qualified seekers, since it is said that *adas* refers to what is remote. The remainder [of the meaning] is that liberation—that is, cessation—from the bondage of the body, which is imagined by ignorance and rooted in nescience, namely from the bondage of the body consisting of egoism and so forth, is indeed accomplished. In the phrase "or whoever" (*yo vā*), the particle *vai* is used for emphasis and should be connected with the end [of the sentence]. In the phrase "only among these" (*eteṣveva*), the emphasis excludes the possibility of being intent upon means other than those already mentioned. ||48||

Now the Guru briefly instructs the disciple regarding the cause of transmigratory existence, its root cause, and the means for its cessation, along with their underlying reasons: "From the union with ignorance...
From the union with ignorance, indeed, there arises for you—the Supreme Self—bondage to the non-self, and from that alone comes transmigratory existence.
The fire of wisdom arising from the discernment of those two shall burn away the effects of ignorance, root and branch. ||49||

The bondage to the non-Self is indeed due to your connection with ignorance regarding the Supreme Self; from that alone comes transmigration. May the fire of awakening, arising from the discrimination between these two, utterly consume the effects of ignorance along with their very roots. (49)
Commentary:

O Supreme Self, due to the conjunction with ignorance—that is, the connection with beginningless nescience—there arises the bondage of the non-self, which is the notion of selfhood regarding the non-self, namely the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. From that very source comes transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), consisting of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of attributes such as birth, old age, death, pleasure, pain, and insentience.

The fire of discernment (*viveka*)—which is the knowledge arisen from the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self—is that fire of realization (*bodhavahni*) produced by such discernment (*bhedajñāna*). It shall burn away, reducing to ashes, the bondage beginning with the ego-sense and ending with the body, along with its seed in the form of ignorance and its effects; it shall utterly consume the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of birth, old age, death, and so forth, which are brought about by that bondage. This is the meaning.

Thus, it has been stated in summary: the cause of transmigratory existence is bondage to the non-Self; the cause of that is the conjunction with ignorance (*ajñāna*); the means for its cessation is the realization of the Supreme Self; and the cause of that is the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. By this, the logical justification has been demonstrated regarding the supreme knowledge born from Vedāntic inquiry as the destroyer of the suffering of *saṃsāra*; for bondage, which arises from ignorance, ceases through knowledge alone and not by any other means. ||49||

Thus delighted by the flow of the nectar of words issuing from the lotus-face of his guru, the disciple—desiring to plunge deeply into the ocean of the ambrosial speech pouring forth without restraint from the jar of that [guru’s] mouth—respectfully requests him to ask [further] in order to shatter all his own doubts.
The disciple said:
"O Lord, please listen; this question is being asked by me."
Having heard your reply from your own mouth, I shall have attained my purpose. (50)
O Master, please listen out of compassion to this question being asked through your mouth; having heard the answer from you, I shall have attained my life's purpose. (50)
Commentary:

By this, the duty of the disciple is taught that one should not pose a question without first informing the Guru. Regarding "the answer to which is the answer": by not saying, "This question is being asked by me," but rather first making the request, "Please listen out of compassion," he indicates—through that speech—the increase of the Guru's affection for him, as well as the Guru's mental gentleness and his own state of eager desire to know. By the phrase "having heard from your mouth," it is made known that he has no other refuge. ||50||
